The unavailable-day SHORT cell trails its control on both runtimes because the dropped Wednesday session leaves the strength week incomplete (E3, SSCTR S-A): conservative and unchanged, but narrower than the contract's E6 example of an unavailable day. In the return's own week the reducer credits post-return exposures as return steps the planner re-based (F1's origin).
rulings.Return base (contract §10.2, T13): Approved: a return resumes the dose last executed; ceilings never above the last executed load; the return load cap holds the logged entry; the S-G entry repetitions now equal the executed ones.
rulings.R42 (contract §10.3): Credit part approved (one exposure later, then progression continues). Repetition part NOT approved: F2. The contract's wording ("a load above the one the state held starts its credit at 0") does not cover an athlete-initiated heavier lift (D44), which still carries the earlier credit on both runtimes (pre-existing, non-blocking).

newFindings.finding: NF-R7ASM-1 (ssctr-r7asm-trace-d47.mjs, round-12 section V): after a 30-day break reported mid-week (RESTART), the race statement states a longest continuous run of 45 and 50 minutes where the athlete has run at most 20 and 15 continuous minutes since the restart (the predecessor states 20 and 15); the value is the restart week's stored planned summary (an easy run of 45/50 minutes dated inside the pause, never executed) applied by the reducer as executed when the post-return easy runs advance; doses unchanged (taper and race-week runs, completion basis, achieved peaks and strides identical in all 8 restart timelines).
newFindings.whyNotBlocking: No dose or calibration changes (race day stays a completion by mode); the athlete-facing statement overstates continuous running two to three times and must be corrected before any athlete-facing use.
newFindings.recommendation: In the return's own week, read the planned summary from the sessions after the return point (C5), or never credit a planned minute as an executed continuous run.

newFindings.finding: NF-R7ASM-3 (part D): week 0 executed but unreviewed with the back squat lifted at 82.5 kg against an 80 kg row (D44, target met); every later week executed as prescribed and reviewed. Rows ["2026-11-11 back-squat 3x5@3 KNOWN 80 KNOWN","2026-11-18 back-squat 3x5@3 KNOWN 80 KNOWN","2026-11-25 back-squat 2x5@3 KNOWN 80 KNOWN","2026-12-02 back-squat 4x5@3 KNOWN 80 KNOWN","2026-12-09 back-squat 4x5@3 KNOWN 82.5 KNOWN","2026-12-16 back-squat 4x5@3 KNOWN 82.5 KNOWN","2026-12-23 back-squat 3x5@3 KNOWN 85 KNOWN","2026-12-30 back-squat 4x5@3 KNOWN 85 KNOWN"]; predecessor ["2026-11-11 back-squat 3x5@3 KNOWN 80 KNOWN","2026-11-18 back-squat 3x5@3 KNOWN 82.5 KNOWN","2026-11-25 back-squat 2x5@3 KNOWN 82.5 KNOWN","2026-12-02 back-squat 4x5@3 KNOWN 82.5 KNOWN","2026-12-09 back-squat 4x5@3 KNOWN 85 KNOWN","2026-12-16 back-squat 4x5@3 KNOWN 85 KNOWN","2026-12-23 back-squat 3x5@3 KNOWN 87.5 KNOWN","2026-12-30 back-squat 4x5@3 KNOWN 87.5 KNOWN"]: the view takes the projection's lower load and resets its credit each week while history holds the higher one, so the load stalls four weeks and stays one step behind.
newFindings.whyNotBlocking: Lower dose only; progression resumes one step behind; no safety cost.
newFindings.recommendation: When the projection holds a load below history's evidence-gated load, plan from history's load and credit (or keep the credit at the projection's load), so earned progression is not withheld.

sources.title: Effects of tapering on performance in endurance athletes: A systematic review and meta-analysis
sources.authors: Wang Z, Wang YT, Gao W, Zhong Y
sources.population_design_dose: 14 studies in well-trained endurance athletes (VO2max >55 ml/kg/min).
sources.findings: Taper improved time-trial (SMD -0.45) and time-to-exhaustion performance; volume reductions of 41-60% with maintained intensity and frequency, durations <=7, 8-14 or 15-21 days and progressive or step tapers were effective.
limitations: Trained, not recreational, athletes; few studies per subgroup.
counterevidence: No change in VO2max or economy; benefits depend on prior overload.

sources.title: Detraining: loss of training-induced physiological and performance adaptations. Part I: short term insufficient training stimulus
sources.authors: Mujika I, Padilla S
sources.population_design_dose: Narrative review of short-term detraining (less than 4 weeks of insufficient training stimulus) in athletes and recently trained individuals.
sources.findings: Short-term cardiorespiratory detraining in highly trained athletes brings a rapid decline in VO2max and blood volume and impaired endurance performance; the changes are more moderate in recently trained individuals; strength declines are limited.
limitations: Narrative review, abstract only; highly trained athletes; no dose rule for the first session back.
counterevidence: Declines are described as rapid in highly trained athletes, so a short break is not free of loss.

sources.title: Effect of short-term training cessation on performance measures in distance runners
sources.authors: Houmard JA, Hortobagyi T, Johns RA, Bruno NJ, Nute CC, Shinebarger MH, Welborn JW
sources.population_design_dose: 12 distance runners; 14 days of training cessation; measures before and after, no control group.
sources.findings: VO2max fell about 4% (61.6 to 58.7 ml/kg/min), time to exhaustion about 9% and submaximal heart rate rose about 6%; running economy did not change; the authors call the VO2max reduction relatively small.
limitations: Abstract only; small uncontrolled sample; 14 days, longer than the short return class.
counterevidence: Time to exhaustion fell more than VO2max, so performance may drop more than VO2max suggests.

sources.title: Two weeks of detraining reduces cardiopulmonary function and muscular fitness in endurance athletes
sources.authors: Chen YT, Hsieh YY, Ho JY, Lin TY, Lin JC
sources.population_design_dose: 15 endurance-trained men aged 19-26; 2 weeks of detraining; measures before and after.
sources.findings: VO2max, time to exhaustion, maximal stroke volume and knee-extensor strength fell significantly after two weeks; muscle endurance was maintained.
limitations: Abstract only; small uncontrolled sample of young men; two weeks, longer than the short return class.
counterevidence: A measurable loss within two weeks argues against treating a short break as no break.

sources.title: Cardiac size and VO2max do not decrease after short-term exercise cessation
sources.authors: Cullinane EM, Sady SP, Vadeboncoeur L, Burke M, Thompson PD
sources.population_design_dose: 15 male competitive distance runners (28 years); 10 days of exercise cessation after 2 weeks of 16 km daily; controlled diet.
sources.findings: Estimated plasma volume fell about 5% and peak exercise heart rate rose about 5%; VO2max, resting heart rate, blood pressure and cardiac dimensions did not change.
limitations: Abstract only; small uncontrolled sample; men only; 1986.
counterevidence: Plasma volume and peak heart rate changed within 10 days.

claims.statement: Intensity maintained while volume falls preserves endurance performance over one to three weeks (R6-S14); a reading that makes exactly one quality session easy is the smallest deviation that meets condition 7, and each FREEZE-A2 reading keeps every run dose at or below the planned dose and the held dose, so none adds intensity or volume.
claims.applicability: Short returns (at most return.shortMaxDays days) meeting other same-week adaptations, and short returns near a race.
limitations: Taper studies in trained athletes; no study of the easy slot itself.
counterevidence: In the fatigue-first and race-crossing readings one more quality session runs easy than strictly needed; the cost is one session.

claims.statement: After at most 10 days without running VO2max was unchanged (R7A-S06), fell about 4% after 14 days (R7A-S04) and two weeks of detraining reduced fitness (R7A-S05); detraining is rapid in highly trained athletes (R7A-S03). One easy session in place of a quality one after a short break is a declared conservative step of small cost either way.
claims.applicability: Short returns.
limitations: Abstracts only; small samples, mostly trained men.
counterevidence: The athlete has usually run two or more sessions after the break before the slot.

claims.statement: Which slot is "the first quality slot" when another adaptation already eased it, when it was made easy and not done, or when only a race touch and the race remain, is not stated by condition 7; the FREEZE-A2 readings are conservative and order-dependent by at most one quality session, and each is a policy declaration to make (R32, R33), not a runtime defect.
limitations: No evidence distinguishes the readings.
counterevidence: None located.

records.applicability: Runtime compositions and readings of declared rules inside the approved envelopes, offline synthetic Node24 reference, stated adult recreational nonclinical V1 population; no real-athlete effect.

decision.rationale: R7ASM-SSCTR-r1 delta check: carries: Short-return grid (315 cases): after the return 0 defects, after the review 0; D58 readings probe, same-day grids and x-sameday byte-identical. One slot per interruption; D58 holds. R7ASE-SSCTR-r1 delta check: carries: short grid, D58 readings and my S1-S10 probe byte-identical; one slot per interruption; the eased slot of a return after unreported weeks follows D58 on the historical quality state (R6-H17). R7AB-SSCTR-r1 delta check: carries: short grid, D58 readings and my S1-S10 probe byte-identical; one slot per interruption. R7AF-SSCTR-r1 delta check: carries: readings unchanged, the short grid and D58 probe byte-identical, one slot per interruption. R7A2-SSCTR-r1 rationale: R7A2-SSCTR-r1 delta check: carries; the readings hold on R7A2-FREEZE-1 (short grid, D58 probe and author combinations byte-identical or equal), and each short break now owns its slot (I9, S-E). R7A1-SSCTR-r2 rationale: All three readings the dossier names are accepted. (a) A run eased by a systemic fatigue report is no longer a quality slot, so the return’s easy slot is the next session that would run at quality dose; in the other order the return’s slot is this week’s and fatigue has nothing more to ease. Both orders keep the fatigue restriction (no quality run after the report) and every dose at or below plan; they differ by one quality session next week (EASY 41 against a held THRESHOLD 41). (b) A skipped session is not a slot: the moved quality run is the slot if the move rule moved it, else next week’s. (c) An easy slot later reported unavailable passes on at the next composition from a later week, the weekly review at the latest; until then next week shows its planned quality run, which is a plan, not an executed dose, under the weekly-review contract. Two readings the dossier does not name are accepted as non-blocking: an easy slot not done does not pass on (the declared missed-session rule: no debt, the next comparable session repeats the held dose, 41, the same dose as when the easy slot was done); and a short break in the taper or race week carries the slot past the race to the first next-block threshold (one session, conservative).
preserve: Exactly one slot is made easy per short return
No quality run follows a systemic fatigue report in the same week, in either order
A skipped session is never a slot; a slot already history stays the slot
Every run dose stays at or below the planned and the held dose
decision.mec_change_level: No change: readings of the declared condition 7 as frozen at R7A1-FREEZE-A2.
decision.trade_off: At most one more quality session runs easy in the fatigue-first and race-crossing readings; the gain is a single, order-proof test of the slot.
must_not: Present any value as validated physiology, an injury-prevention threshold, a readiness score or a guarantee.
Substitute a training dose for clinical assessment.
Treat missing data as adverse or as tolerance.
Change official plan state or completed history.
conditions: Scope: offline synthetic Node24 reference only, for the adult (18+) recreational nonclinical V1 population; no real-athlete effect.

This approval excludes a stored load tick that counts an exposure the projection assumed and the athlete did not execute (NF-R7ASE-3, R42).

The start state of a return is the state at its interruption under R7A2-SSCTR-INTERRUPTION-STATE (revision R7ASM-SSCTR-r1), INTERRUPTION_EPISODE_CONTRACT R7AF-INTERRUPTION-1, WEEK_START_AUTHORITY_CONTRACT R7AB-WEEKSTART-1 (its record, temporal-contradiction rule and boundaries B1-B7, B9-B11) and STATE_MODEL_CONTRACT R7ASM-STATE-MODEL-1 (which replaces STATE_EVIDENCE_CONTRACT R7ASE-STATE-EVIDENCE-1): a correction names its interruption (episodeId) or repeats its days and starts from what the athlete had executed at its own start; a break after a re-entry or after training is new and starts from that re-entry plus the facts executed since; the state at the interruption is read value by value (one value per strength exercise, one for the run): a stored value counts only when its start holds that value as evidence decided before the cut (the intake, a return’s entry, the weekly review’s rule on that value’s historical value, or a projection whose own base value was historical and that the week before executed per sport exactly as assumed, loads included); a value a review carried from a projection is rebuilt by the review’s rule on its historical value; otherwise the value moves back to its last such start and the sessions executed after it are facts only (a known load lifted is the load under D44; a projected dose lifted is that load with its repetition target, never a load tick only the projection counted); weeks never reported are not history; a named correction that contradicts its own executed re-entry is asked; anything else is asked; each short break owns its easy slot.

Weekly-review contract: these readings hold when every elapsed week receives a gating weekly review, in order and after its last session; a week that receives no gating review keeps the projection’s assumption, and a skipped easy slot then reaches next week only at a composition from a later week (E3; R18, Engineering with Product/Data).

answers.answer: At HISTORICAL-PROJECTION-FREEZE-1: adequate for this record's scope (its grids and probes hold, see the rationale); the freeze as a whole is NOT_READY on F1, F2 and F3. At STATE-EVIDENCE-FREEZE-1: adequate; the value-scoped history leaves the planner, the return recipe, ceilings, restoration and short return unchanged (byte-identical grids; R5, profiles and simulations identical) and only changes which executed state a return starts from. At R7A-BOUNDARY-FINAL-FREEZE: adequate; the week-start authority change leaves the return recipe, ceilings, restoration and short return unchanged (byte-identical grids) and only moves a return's start back to an executed state. At R7A-FINAL-FREEZE: adequate; the identity and state change leaves the return recipe, ceilings, restoration and short return unchanged (byte-identical grids). R7A2-SSCTR-r1: At R7A2-FREEZE-1: adequate; the start state of a return is the state at the break (D59 closed). R7A1-SSCTR-r2: Adequate: after a short return the week keeps one easy slot and every other session of the plan.
Material facts: the return report’s clock and break length, same-week reports with their clocks, and executed sessions from the ledger (provenance kept).
KEEP of the frozen readings is defensible; unknown: individual tolerance of the first quality session after a short break.
Against R7A1-FREEZE-A1 the change was necessary (no slot when the week’s slot was past, D58); against FREEZE-A2 no further change is needed.
The smallest sufficient intervention is one easy slot, the first quality slot still ahead in the week as it stands, carried to the next week placed.
A position-based reading (a fatigue-eased run counts as the slot) is about as small but is a policy declaration (R32); nothing smaller meets condition 7.
It protects the return’s conservative step and the stated progression; the cost is at most one quality session.

sources.title: The Duration of the Repeated-Bout Effect After Eccentric Exercise
sources.authors: Theodorou AA, Margaritelis NV, Karyofyllidou AV, Christodoulou F, Jamurtas AZ, et al.
sources.population_design_dose: 48 young recreationally active men; two identical bouts of maximal eccentric knee-extensor exercise (5 x 15 repetitions); after the first bout participants were randomly allocated to repeat it after 3, 6, 9 or 12 weeks (12 completers per group).
sources.findings: The repeated-bout effect (smaller losses of torque and range of motion, less soreness and muscle damage) was evident at 3 and 6 weeks for most outcomes, remained detectable at 9 weeks for selected markers, and was no longer meaningfully present at 12 weeks.
sources.locator: Abstract; Methods 2.2 (random allocation to the interval groups); Results (Table 2, model-estimated contrasts by interval); Discussion (earlier downhill-running and elbow-flexor studies); Limitations (ssctr-evidence/PMC13674372.xml).
limitations: Maximal unaccustomed eccentric knee-extensor work in young men; resistance training at 2-3 reps in reserve damages muscle far less; markers assessed on days 2 and 4 only; activity between bouts not monitored.
counterevidence: Earlier studies cited in the discussion found protection that faded by 9 weeks after downhill running and persisted partly to 10 weeks for the elbow flexors.

sources.title: American College of Sports Medicine Position Stand. Resistance Training Prescription for Muscle Function, Hypertrophy, and Physical Performance in Healthy Adults: An Overview of Reviews
sources.authors: Currier BS, D'Souza AC, Singh MAF, Lowisz CV, Rawson ES, Schoenfeld BJ, Smith-Ryan AE, et al.
sources.population_design_dose: Overview of 137 systematic reviews of randomized trials in healthy adults (>=18 y), resistance training >=6 wk; most evidence from novice trainees.
sources.findings: Resistance training improves strength and hypertrophy versus control; strength enhanced by heavier loads, 2-3 sets, >=2 sessions/wk and exercise at session start; hypertrophy by >=10 sets/muscle/wk; training to failure and periodization not consistently influential; perceived-exertion scales can raise absolute load with strength gains; individualization encouraged for adherence.
sources.locator: Abstract; Results (strength, hypertrophy); Discussion subsections Progressive overload, Specificity/Individualization, Variation.
limitations: Overview of reviews dominated by novice trainees; not concurrent-training or runner specific.
No per-session increment, establishment or return procedure is specified.
counterevidence: States progression is not always necessary for benefit, so planned progression is a choice, not a requirement.

sources.title: Temporal Pattern of the Repeated Bout Effect of Eccentric Exercise on Delayed-Onset Muscle Soreness
sources.authors: Cleary MA, Kimura IF, Sitler MR, Kendrick ZV
sources.population_design_dose: 31 untrained adults (16 men, 15 women); two identical eccentric bouts separated by 6, 7, 8 or 9 weeks; perceived pain (VAS) and tenderness (pressure gauge) before and 0-72 h after each bout.
sources.findings: Perceived pain and tenderness were significantly lower after the second bout; the authors conclude that one eccentric bout 6 to 9 weeks earlier is an effective prophylaxis for soreness from a similar bout.
limitations: Abstract only (PubMed efetch); soreness endpoints only; unaccustomed eccentric work, not effort-guided resistance training at 3 reps in reserve; no set-count progression studied.
counterevidence: Protection was shown for soreness after an identical bout; it says nothing about a larger set count at an effort-chosen load.

sources.title: Muscle damage and inflammation after eccentric exercise: can the repeated bout effect be removed?
sources.authors: Margaritelis NV, Theodorou AA, Baltzopoulos V, Maganaris CN, Paschalis V, Kyparos A, Nikolaidis MG
sources.population_design_dose: 17 young men randomized to alternating eccentric-concentric or eccentric-only isokinetic knee-extensor training for 8 weeks; damage and inflammation markers at weeks 1, 5 and 10.
sources.findings: Concentric training between eccentric blocks markedly reduced the repeated-bout effect, returning muscle toward an unaccustomed state; the protection depends on what is done between bouts.
limitations: Abstract only; isokinetic laboratory protocol; men only.
counterevidence: In a break no training intervenes, so the removal mechanism it shows does not apply during the break itself.

One directed PubMed search on the duration of the repeated-bout effect in untrained or briefly trained people, counterevidence sought in the same query (R7A1-S06: protection can be removed by what is done between bouts). claims.statement: The declared recipe (strengthReturnSets) applies to every exercise executed before a moderate or long break: entry at strengthEntrySets with strengthEntryMinimumRir or more, step 2, at most one set per executed whole week up to the last count executed before the break, above it only through a later completed development block, and no set for the block in progress. R7A2-FREEZE-1 applies all four to exercises first executed in the break’s week (first-week grid E = O = B = 0 for every class; extended grid over 1,377 cases with ceiling equality; restoration-grid returns with ceiling equality). Repeated-bout protection fades over weeks (R6-S48), the reasoning of D53, D55, D56, D57 and D59.
claims.applicability: Moderate or long returns whose break week holds executed exposures, first exposures included.
limitations: R6-S48 studied maximal eccentric bouts, not effort-guided training at 3 or more reps in reserve.
Synthetic grids; FIXED rotation except a 24-case rotation spot-check.
counterevidence: One bout protects for weeks (R6-S48 at 3-6 weeks; R7A1-S05 at 6-9 weeks, abstract), so the physiological size of the bypass D59 removed was modest; the closure is about the declared rule.

claims.statement: Two sets at an effort-chosen load with 3 or more reps in reserve is inside the position stand’s range for novices (R6-S01); the boundaries that still give a first establishment (NF-1, S-H) therefore carry a modest physiological risk, the same as any new exercise.
claims.applicability: Sporting weight of the remaining boundaries.
limitations: Position stand evidence is for continuous training, not returns.
counterevidence: Protection depends on what is done between bouts (R7A1-S06, abstract).

claims.statement: Under Founder request R7-A.1 §10 and R7-A.2 §13/§22, D53 closes when no known equivalent state mode allows a restoration jump. None remains: a session on a break’s stated first day and executions logged after the return leave the return without a pre-break count for those exercises (Founder I4, I6, P4; the record as reported), so no declared ceiling is bypassed; they get the untrained establishment, and a newer report of the same break restores the entry and ceiling (I2).
claims.applicability: D53 status and the R7-A exit.
limitations: A governance criterion, not physiology; the boundaries are Product/UX and Data questions (NF-1, R37).
counterevidence: Physically the same-day session happened before the athlete stopped; a reading that starts the break after it would keep the exposure (NF-1).

records.applicability: Runtime compositions and readings of declared rules inside the approved envelopes, offline synthetic Node24 reference, stated adult recreational nonclinical V1 population; no real-athlete effect.

decision.rationale: R7ASM-SSCTR-r1 delta check: carries, closed for its scope (D59): First-week grid D59 (306 cases): {"NONE":{"cases":90,"exercises":264,"E":0,"O":0,"B":0,"casesWithAny":0},"FAMILIAR":{"cases":108,"exercises":408,"E":0,"O":0,"B":0,"casesWithAny":0},"KNOWN":{"cases":108,"exercises":408,"E":0,"O":0,"B":0,"casesWithAny":0}} (byte-identical); extended first-week grid (1377 cases): E 0, O 0, B 0, CEQ 0, NOENTRY 0, BLK 0, the tallies identical; one informational difference (maxBeforeLimit of fx-FAMILIAR-RUNNING_SUPPORT-2-20-b1/MISSED: db-row and db-bench-press 1 -> 2, inside their declared fallback ceiling, O 0); ceiling equality 0 disagreements (byte-identical). The general D53 question is answered by F1 (a return-step mode, recorded under REGAIN-BASE and CYCLE2-COMPOSITIONS), not by the first-week mode this record rules on. R7ASE-SSCTR-r1 delta check: carries, closed: the first-week, extended, ceiling and same-day grids are byte-identical; the state at the break now reads each value from evidence and takes a lifted known load as the load (SE-C), never a projected one. R7AB-SSCTR-r1 delta check: carries, closed: the first-week, extended and ceiling grids and the same-day grid are byte-identical; on a never-logged program the point is now the intake, so an exercise never performed enters by the first-exposure establishment (the NONE-class reading), never as a return of a count it never executed. R7AF-SSCTR-r1 delta check: carries, closed: the first-week, extended and ceiling grids are byte-identical, and the first-day boundary (NF-1) is now ordered by the stated start time or asked, never read silently. R7A2-SSCTR-r1 rationale: D59 is closed. R7A2-FREEZE-1 starts a return from the state at the break: the start of its week, or the start a return still in force set, advanced by the exposures executed before the break’s first day as facts only. Every exercise executed before the break is in use with its last performed date and its last executed whole count (target met, outside a phase reduction) as the ceiling; moderate and long returns enter it at the entry; the block in progress earns no set; no count rises faster than one set per executed whole week. Founder §13 is met on my unchanged instrument (E = O = B = 0 for NONE and FAMILIAR, O = 0 for KNOWN), on an extended grid (moderate, long, the 28/29-day boundary, missed targets; ceiling equality) and on later-week returns (1,090 exercises, ceiling equality). The R6 round-11 narrowing of R7A1-SSCTR-r2 is now implemented: pause-week progression stays unapplied, pause-week facts are kept. Two boundaries remain outside D59 because the return holds no pre-break count for those exercises (a session on the break’s stated first day; executions logged after the return): they are Product/UX and Data questions with a working correction path, not restoration modes.
preserve: The progression the break week’s pre-break exposures earned stays unapplied: no load adoption, gate step, cap rise or end, return step or block set (Founder I7)
Exercises never executed before the break keep the R23 reading (no ceiling, establishment by effort)
Return entry and step 2 for every exercise in use
decision.mec_change_level: None further: the R7-A.2 runtime change to the start state of a return is accepted; no policy text, no new rule.
decision.trade_off: Exercises first done in the break week re-enter one set lower and stay at their pre-break count until a later completed development block; restoration is slower (cost R35), never faster than declared.
must_not: Present any value as validated physiology, an injury-prevention threshold, a readiness score or a guarantee.
Substitute a training dose for clinical assessment.
Treat missing data as adverse or as tolerance.
Change official plan state or completed history.

D59 (met at R7A2-FREEZE-1 and at R7A-FINAL-FREEZE and at R7A-BOUNDARY-FINAL-FREEZE and at STATE-EVIDENCE-FREEZE-1 and at HISTORICAL-PROJECTION-FREEZE-1, closed): a return starts from the state at the break (stateAtBreak, strengthAtBreak): every exercise executed before the break’s first day is in use with its last performed date and, outside a return step and a phase reduction, its last executed whole count after the time fit (target met) as the ceiling (the largest of the break week, R20); a moderate or long return enters it at strengthEntrySets with strengthEntryMinimumRir or more, step 2 follows, the block in progress earns no set and the count comes back at most one set per executed whole week up to the ceiling; the progression the pre-break exposures earned stays unapplied. Regression: ssctr-r7a1-recheck-firstweek.mjs with E, O and B at 0 for NONE and FAMILIAR and O at 0 for KNOWN, my restoration, cap and short grids, and test "R7-A.2 I4/I5/I8 (SSCTR D59)". R7ASE-SSCTR-r1: the state at the break also takes the load the athlete lifted on a known-load row as the exercise’s load (lighter, or heavier only under D44: at most one smallest increment above the row and the row’s target met), a fact and never a step; an effort-guided row adopts nothing; a projected dose lifted exactly is that load with its repetition target and no further step. This approval excludes a stored load tick that counts an exposure the projection assumed and the athlete did not execute (NF-R7ASE-3, R42).

Supersedes in part the R6 round-11 acceptance "Sessions before the pause, in the pause week": the progression of the break week’s pre-break exposures stays unapplied for every exercise; their facts (in use, last performed date, last executed whole count) are kept for every exercise, first exposures included.

A strength session on an interruption’s first day is ordered by the interruption’s stated start time: a session completed before that time is in the state (entry, that day’s count as the ceiling), one completed after it is not; with dates only it is asked when its order changes a fact the return starts from (in use, ceiling, unlogged load), and when only a last performed date differs the earlier date is kept (the conservative reading for a re-establishment threshold). This replaces the R7-A.2 NF-1 boundary.

Training before the latest interruption logged after its return is confirmed first: while that return sets the plan (its re-entry week), every other report asks to confirm the interruption again, and the newer report reads the whole record (entry and ceiling as read in time). This replaces the R7-A.2 S-H/R37 boundary; the cost of what the pending question holds back is NF-R7AF-1 (routed, R38).
Weekly-review contract as in every record (R18).

answers.answer: At HISTORICAL-PROJECTION-FREEZE-1: adequate for this record's scope (its grids and probes hold, see the rationale); the freeze as a whole is NOT_READY on F1, F2 and F3. At STATE-EVIDENCE-FREEZE-1: adequate; the value-scoped history leaves the planner, the return recipe, ceilings, restoration and short return unchanged (byte-identical grids; R5, profiles and simulations identical) and only changes which executed state a return starts from. At R7A-BOUNDARY-FINAL-FREEZE: adequate; the week-start authority change leaves the return recipe, ceilings, restoration and short return unchanged (byte-identical grids) and only moves a return's start back to an executed state. At R7A-FINAL-FREEZE: adequate; the identity and state change leaves the return recipe, ceilings, restoration and short return unchanged (byte-identical grids). R7A2-SSCTR-r1: Adequate to the declared recipe after a moderate or long return, the first loaded week included: entry, step 2, ceiling and the block-in-progress rule are applied.
Material facts: executions before the break’s first day (ledger provenance, read as the weekly review reads them) and the break’s class.
KEEP of R7A2-FREEZE-1 is defensible; unknown: the protection one pre-break week gives and how often the boundaries occur.
No further change is necessary: the comparator (the same exercise executed one week earlier) and the first-week case now get the same return steps.
The change made is the smallest sufficient one: facts kept, progression not applied.
Capping only the jump would have left the entry and the block set wrong; replaying the week’s review would have laundered progression (I7).
It protects the restoration ceiling (I8) without changing the progression of exercises already in state.
Declared rule plus repeated-bout duration (R6-S48 full text; R7A1-S05 abstract), which lowers the physiological size.
R7ASM-SSCTR-r1: material uncertainty remains in real use (synthetic probes only); How much one pre-break week protects a novice; the real frequency of the boundaries.
No ASK, HOLD or clinical routing for the ruling: eligibility as before; a clinical reason routes as before. NF-1 recommends an ASK when a break’s stated first day holds an executed session.

sources.title: The Duration of the Repeated-Bout Effect After Eccentric Exercise
sources.authors: Theodorou AA, Margaritelis NV, Karyofyllidou AV, Christodoulou F, Jamurtas AZ, et al.
sources.population_design_dose: 48 young recreationally active men; two identical bouts of maximal eccentric knee-extensor exercise (5 x 15 repetitions); after the first bout participants were randomly allocated to repeat it after 3, 6, 9 or 12 weeks (12 completers per group).
sources.findings: The repeated-bout effect (smaller losses of torque and range of motion, less soreness and muscle damage) was evident at 3 and 6 weeks for most outcomes, remained detectable at 9 weeks for selected markers, and was no longer meaningfully present at 12 weeks.
sources.locator: Abstract; Methods 2.2 (random allocation to the interval groups); Results (Table 2, model-estimated contrasts by interval); Discussion (earlier downhill-running and elbow-flexor studies); Limitations (ssctr-evidence/PMC13674372.xml).
limitations: Maximal unaccustomed eccentric knee-extensor work in young men; resistance training at 2-3 reps in reserve damages muscle far less; markers assessed on days 2 and 4 only; activity between bouts not monitored.
counterevidence: Earlier studies cited in the discussion found protection that faded by 9 weeks after downhill running and persisted partly to 10 weeks for the elbow flexors.

sources.title: Gaining more from doing less? The effects of a one-week deload period during supervised resistance training on muscular adaptations
sources.authors: Coleman M, Burke R, Augustin F, Pinero A, Maldonado J, Fisher JP, Israetel M, et al.
sources.population_design_dose: 39 resistance-trained young men and women; 9-week high-volume program; one group abstained from training for 1 week at the midpoint and then resumed the same program, the other trained continuously.
sources.findings: No appreciable between-group differences in lower-body muscle size, local endurance or power; the continuous group improved isometric and dynamic lower-body strength more than the deload group.
sources.locator: Abstract; Methods (group allocation, deload at the midpoint); Results; Limitations (ssctr-evidence/PMC10809978.xml).
limitations: The deload was complete cessation, not a set reduction; resistance-trained young adults; upper-body training unsupervised.
counterevidence: Strength gains were smaller after one week without training, so breaks are not neutral for strength.

sources.title: Comparative effects of single vs. multiple-set resistance training on neuromuscular performance and muscle morphology in sedentary men
sources.authors: Coskun IA, Kafkas ME
sources.population_design_dose: 34 sedentary young men randomized (computer-generated sequence, sealed opaque envelopes) to single-set, three-set or control; 8 weeks, twice weekly, seven exercises of up to 10 repetitions.
sources.findings: Both single-set and three-set training improved strength, power and muscle size over 8 weeks; three sets gave larger gains (squat 1-RM +14.8% and leg cross-sectional area +11.3%, against about 6-8% with one set), a volume dose-response from the first weeks.
sources.locator: Abstract; Methods (randomization, concealed allocation, training programme); Results; Conclusions (ssctr-evidence/PMC13670784.xml).
limitations: Small sample; men only; participants and trainers not blinded; retrospectively registered; eight weeks.
counterevidence: A lower set count costs some adaptation if it persists, so a reduction is acceptable only when it is short.

sources.title: The repeated bout effect of traditional resistance exercises on running performance across 3 bouts
sources.authors: Doma K, Schumann M, Leicht AS, Heilbronn BE, Damas F, Burt D
sources.population_design_dose: 12 resistance-untrained men; three lower-body 6RM sessions; damage markers and submaximal and maximal running at 24 and 48 h.
sources.findings: The first bout raised creatine kinase most; at least two bouts were needed before soreness, range of motion and submaximal running were protected; the authors advise avoiding submaximal running for at least 48 h after resistance training until the third bout.
limitations: Abstract only; untrained men; 6RM sessions.
counterevidence: Protection appeared after two bouts, so a single earlier block of training may already have conferred some.

sources.title: Comparison between high- and low-intensity eccentric cycling of equal mechanical work for muscle damage and the repeated bout effect
sources.authors: Mavropalias G, Koeda T, Barley OR, Poon WCK, Fisher AJ, Blazevich AJ, Nosaka K
sources.population_design_dose: 20 men; two eccentric cycling bouts 2 weeks apart: high-intensity twice (1 min x 5 at 20% of peak power, n = 11) or low-intensity first (4 min x 5 at 5% of peak power, matched mechanical work) then high-intensity (n = 9).
sources.findings: Both first bouts lowered knee-extensor torque and jump height similarly at 24 h, and both groups lost less function after the second bout. Soreness after the first bout was greater after high intensity (peak 4.2 vs 1.4), but after the second, high-intensity bout it was greater in the group whose first bout was low-intensity (3.6 vs 1.5).
limitations: Abstract only; eccentric cycling, not resistance training; allocation method not stated in the abstract; small groups; men only.
counterevidence: A low-intensity first bout protected function but gave less protection against soreness than a full first bout; soreness after the second bout (3.6) stayed below that after an unprotected high-intensity first bout (4.2).

sources.title: The Effect of Load and Volume Autoregulation on Muscular Strength and Hypertrophy: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
sources.authors: Hickmott LM, Chilibeck PD, Shaw KA, Butcher SJ
sources.population_design_dose: 15 studies in resistance-trained individuals: six on load autoregulation (RIR-based RPE, velocity) against percentage-based loading, nine on volume autoregulation by velocity-loss thresholds.
sources.findings: Autoregulated and standardized load prescription gave similar 1RM gains (MD 2.07 kg, 95% CI -0.32 to 4.46); velocity-loss thresholds of 25% or less favoured strength and higher thresholds hypertrophy.
sources.locator: Abstract (PubMed efetch, reviews/ssctr-r7a1-abstracts.out.txt); PMCID PMC8762534 not read.
limitations: Abstract only; trained individuals; no study of logged-load adoption or of a lighter load chosen by the athlete.
counterevidence: Similar mean gains do not show that adopting a lighter self-chosen load is neutral for every athlete.

claims.statement: Repeated-bout protection is evident 3-6 weeks after a bout and largely gone by 12 weeks (R6-S48), and one week without training cost some strength gain (R6-S45); after a gap long enough to need re-establishment the earlier count comes back gradually, and a week whose last executed exposure was reduced (by its phase or a fatigue report) or fitted below its count is no evidence that the capped count was executed and tolerated, so it neither raises nor ends the cap. Holding costs at most one set for one more week.
claims.applicability: Regain and return caps under phase, fatigue and time-budget reductions.
limitations: Maximal eccentric work in young men (R6-S48); trained young adults (R6-S45); the cap is a declared heuristic, not a threshold.
counterevidence: Under a persistent tight budget the last session of the week may always be trimmed, so the cap holds although an earlier session executed the whole count (R30).

claims.statement: The declared return rule lets the count come back at most one set per executed week and go above the ceiling only through a later development block (strengthReturnSets); a cap that ends against the ending week’s count while the same transition adds a block-boundary set lets the count come back two sets at once (1 to 3), the jump the declared rule excludes; the repeated-bout reasoning of D53, D55 and D56 applies (R6-S48; R6-S55 and R7A-S01 at abstract level).
claims.applicability: Return caps whose ceiling is below the normal count (a pre-break count fitted to the time budget, R20).
limitations: R6-S55 and R7A-S01 are abstract-only; the athlete has trained at the capped count for several weeks before the jump, which lowers but does not remove the concern.
counterevidence: Several weeks of one-set exposures give some protection; the size of the residual risk of a 1-to-3 jump is unknown.

claims.statement: Single-set training improves strength and size, three sets more (R6-S52); a set held back for longer under the last-exposure reading costs some adaptation if it persists, which is a progression trade-off, not a safety one.
claims.applicability: Persistent time-budget configurations (R30).
limitations: Sedentary young men, 8 weeks.
counterevidence: The held set returns as soon as the last session of a week fits its count.

claims.statement: Autoregulated (RIR-based) load prescription gives strength gains similar to percentage-based prescription in trained individuals (R7A1-S04), consistent with gating set-count restoration on executed exposures rather than on calendar time; no study tests which session of a week should gate it.
claims.applicability: Background for S1 only.
limitations: Abstract only.
counterevidence: None located.

claims.statement: No study tests set-count regain under time budgets or the choice between the last and any session of a week; these remain declared heuristics.
limitations: Negative directed search (Q2) at abstract level.
counterevidence: None located.

records.applicability: Runtime compositions and readings of declared rules inside the approved envelopes, offline synthetic Node24 reference, stated adult recreational nonclinical V1 population; no real-athlete effect.

decision.rationale: R7ASM-SSCTR-r1 delta check: carries: no cap rises or ends after a week whose last exposure was not whole (restoration grid 0 of 4372); E6 credits a fatigue-reduced return-step week by the review's rule and the cap stays one set lower (2 against 3). R7ASE-SSCTR-r1 delta check: carries: no cap rises or ends after a week whose last exposure was not whole (grids byte-identical). R7AB-SSCTR-r1 delta check: carries: no cap rises or ends after a week whose last exposure was not whole (grids byte-identical). R7AF-SSCTR-r1 delta check: carries: no cap rises or ends after a week whose last exposure was not whole (grids and the D56 author grid byte-identical). R7A2-SSCTR-r1 rationale: R7A2-SSCTR-r1 delta check: carries: no cap rises or ends after a week whose last exposure was not whole, no covered count comes back more than one set above the largest since the return, and the D56 author grid holds (206 to 200 trimmed cap-weeks, 0 rises or ends after them). R7A1-SSCTR-r2 rationale: R7A1-SSCTR-r2 delta check: carries with D57 now met: no cap rises or ends after a week whose last exposure was not whole, and no covered count comes back more than one set above the largest since the return. R7A1-SSCTR-r1 rationale: "An executed exposure" means the last executed exposure, the one that gives the week’s counts (R19): that is the reading of REGAIN-BASE condition 5 and ITEMS-5-8 item 7, and the only one that keeps FR2 when a fatigue report reduces the last session of a cap week (QE-R7A-22, verified on both runtimes). "Any" would release a cap a later reduction holds; "last" is never less conservative than a reading that also counts an earlier whole session. The formulation is approved and R7A1-FREEZE-A1 meets it for the rise of both caps and for the regain cap. It does not meet it for the end of the return cap: the cap ends against the ending week’s normal count, after weeks fitted below their count and at block boundaries that add a set, so a count comes back 1 to 3 (D57, blocking: a known equivalent path of D53). The cost of "last" under a persistent tight budget is recorded as R30 (non-blocking).
preserve: A time fit is not a phase reduction for the phase reading and for the return ceiling (R20)
A fatigue or phase reduction of the last executed exposure holds the cap (FR2)
One reading of every representation: a row without counts reads its week’s planned counts
The count after a re-establishment or a return comes back at most one set per executed week
decision.mec_change_level: No policy change; one blocking runtime change (D57) to the end of the caps; the rise is approved as frozen.
decision.trade_off: No cap rises or ends on unexecuted or reduced work, at the cost of a slower regain when the last session of a week is trimmed while an earlier one fits (R30).
must_not: Present any value as validated physiology, an injury-prevention threshold, a readiness score or a guarantee.
Substitute a training dose for clinical assessment.
Treat missing data as adverse or as tolerance.
Change official plan state or completed history.
conditions: Scope: offline synthetic Node24 reference only, for the adult (18+) recreational nonclinical V1 population stated in PROGRAM_POLICY_R6.population. Missing current eligibility is ASK; pain, injury, illness, functional limitation or a clinical interruption reason is CLINICAL_HUMAN_REQUIRED with no substitute dose.

The regain cap after a re-establishment and the return cap at and after the end of the return steps rise by one set only after a week whose last executed exposure of the exercise, the one that gives the week’s counts (R19, INV-04), did its whole count (its count before the phase reduction) after its time fit; "an executed exposure" in R7A-SSCTR-r2 condition 9 means this exposure (met at R7A1-FREEZE-A1 and at R7A1-FREEZE-A2 and at R7A2-FREEZE-1 and at R7A-FINAL-FREEZE and at R7A-BOUNDARY-FINAL-FREEZE and at STATE-EVIDENCE-FREEZE-1 and at HISTORICAL-PROJECTION-FREEZE-1).
A time fit stays a non-reduction for the phase reading and for the return ceiling (R20); a fatigue or phase reduction of the last executed exposure holds the cap (FR2, QE-R7A-22) (met).
A row written before R7-A, which states no counts, reads its week’s planned counts, so every representation reads the same (met).

D57 (met at R7A1-FREEZE-A2 and at R7A2-FREEZE-1 and at R7A-FINAL-FREEZE and at R7A-BOUNDARY-FINAL-FREEZE and at STATE-EVIDENCE-FREEZE-1 and at HISTORICAL-PROJECTION-FREEZE-1): the return cap rises and ends only after a week whose last executed exposure did its whole count after its time fit, and ends only when it is at or above next week’s normal count with the block-boundary set that transition earns (phase reductions on top); the regain cap ends only at the largest count the exercise can have. No count after a re-establishment or a return exceeds the largest count executed since then by more than one set, for every exercise a cap or the return steps cover (B = 0 over the 864 and 360 timelines of my grids). The end test reads next week’s count as this week’s normal count plus the block set; another rise of the normal count at a transition (the NONE-class first-block clamp, a priorSets regain) was not reached with a cap in force (observation N4). Regression: the grid’s A, B and C at 0 and test "R7-A.1 D57" (both parts).

D59 (met at R7A2-FREEZE-1 and at R7A-FINAL-FREEZE and at R7A-BOUNDARY-FINAL-FREEZE and at STATE-EVIDENCE-FREEZE-1 and at HISTORICAL-PROJECTION-FREEZE-1, closed): a return starts from the state at the break (stateAtBreak, strengthAtBreak): every exercise executed before the break’s first day is in use with its last performed date and, outside a return step and a phase reduction, its last executed whole count after the time fit (target met) as the ceiling (the largest of the break week, R20); a moderate or long return enters it at strengthEntrySets with strengthEntryMinimumRir or more, step 2 follows, the block in progress earns no set and the count comes back at most one set per executed whole week up to the ceiling; the progression the pre-break exposures earned stays unapplied. Regression: ssctr-r7a1-recheck-firstweek.mjs with E, O and B at 0 for NONE and FAMILIAR and O at 0 for KNOWN, my restoration, cap and short grids, and test "R7-A.2 I4/I5/I8 (SSCTR D59)". R7ASE-SSCTR-r1: the state at the break also takes the load the athlete lifted on a known-load row as the exercise’s load (lighter, or heavier only under D44: at most one smallest increment above the row and the row’s target met), a fact and never a step; an effort-guided row adopts nothing; a projected dose lifted exactly is that load with its repetition target and no further step. This approval excludes a stored load tick that counts an exposure the projection assumed and the athlete did not execute (NF-R7ASE-3, R42).

The start state of a return is the state at its interruption under R7A2-SSCTR-INTERRUPTION-STATE (revision R7ASM-SSCTR-r1), INTERRUPTION_EPISODE_CONTRACT R7AF-INTERRUPTION-1, WEEK_START_AUTHORITY_CONTRACT R7AB-WEEKSTART-1 (its record, temporal-contradiction rule and boundaries B1-B7, B9-B11) and STATE_MODEL_CONTRACT R7ASM-STATE-MODEL-1 (which replaces STATE_EVIDENCE_CONTRACT R7ASE-STATE-EVIDENCE-1): a correction names its interruption (episodeId) or repeats its days and starts from what the athlete had executed at its own start; a break after a re-entry or after training is new and starts from that re-entry plus the facts executed since; the state at the interruption is read value by value (one value per strength exercise, one for the run): a stored value counts only when its start holds that value as evidence decided before the cut (the intake, a return’s entry, the weekly review’s rule on that value’s historical value, or a projection whose own base value was historical and that the week before executed per sport exactly as assumed, loads included); a value a review carried from a projection is rebuilt by the review’s rule on its historical value; otherwise the value moves back to its last such start and the sessions executed after it are facts only (a known load lifted is the load under D44; a projected dose lifted is that load with its repetition target, never a load tick only the projection counted); weeks never reported are not history; a named correction that contradicts its own executed re-entry is asked; anything else is asked; each short break owns its easy slot.

Weekly-review contract: these bindings hold when every elapsed week receives a gating weekly review, in order and after its last session, with unreported sessions reviewed as missed. A week that receives no gating review keeps the projection's assumption that it was executed and logged (establishment, progression, block credit, achieved peaks and the strength resume clock); that path is outside this approval and must be closed before any use beyond the offline reference (R18).

confidence.rationale: R7ASM-SSCTR-r1: the grids and probes this record rests on were re-run on both runtimes. The formulation question is settled by my own earlier conditions and verified on both runtimes through the real review path; the D57 mechanism is traced on both runtimes and reproduced in 38 grid cases; the sporting basis is indirect (repeated-bout and detraining evidence), and the heuristic itself is a declared rule.

limitations: Synthetic timelines only; no real-athlete outcome.
The D57 cases need a tight budget (20 minutes, RUNNING_SUPPORT) before the break and more time after it; the author’s 25-35 minute grid does not reach them.
R30: "last" can hold a cap for as long as the last session of the week stays trimmed.
The weekly-review contract (R18) is assumed throughout.
R7ASM-SSCTR-r1: synthetic offline probes only; the findings are demonstrated on my own scenarios and on the corpus, not on real athletes.

answers.answer: At HISTORICAL-PROJECTION-FREEZE-1: adequate for this record's scope (its grids and probes hold, see the rationale); the freeze as a whole is NOT_READY on F1, F2 and F3. At STATE-EVIDENCE-FREEZE-1: adequate; the value-scoped history leaves the planner, the return recipe, ceilings, restoration and short return unchanged (byte-identical grids; R5, profiles and simulations identical) and only changes which executed state a return starts from. At R7A-BOUNDARY-FINAL-FREEZE: adequate; the week-start authority change leaves the return recipe, ceilings, restoration and short return unchanged (byte-identical grids) and only moves a return's start back to an executed state. At R7A-FINAL-FREEZE: adequate; the identity and state change leaves the return recipe, ceilings, restoration and short return unchanged (byte-identical grids). R7A2-SSCTR-r1: At R7A2-FREEZE-1: adequate; the start state of a return is the state at the break (D59 closed). R7A1-SSCTR-r2: At R7A1-FREEZE-A2: adequate (D57 and D58 met); the start state of a return is outside this record (D59). R7A1-SSCTR-r1: Adequate for the rise of both caps and for the regain cap; not adequate for the end of the return cap (D57).

The material facts are the executed rows of the week with their counts before the phase reduction, after it and after the fit, the cap and ceiling in the state, and the block boundary; all synthetic, with provenance in the probes.
KEEP of the frozen rise is defensible; KEEP of the frozen end is not, because it lets a count come back two sets at once.
Against R7A-FREEZE-2 the change is necessary (a trimmed week released the cap: 2 to 4); against "any" it is necessary for FR2.
The smallest sufficient change is the frozen rise plus one end condition (D57).
Reading "any" breaks FR2; a combined reading (last not reduced, any whole) is less conservative and not needed for safety; leaving the end as frozen keeps the 1-to-3 jump.
Yes: progression continues one set per whole week; the cost is a slower regain under persistent trims (R30).
The direction is supported with limits (R6-S48, R6-S45; R6-S55 and R7A-S01 at abstract level); no source decides the choice of session.
R7ASM-SSCTR-r1: material uncertainty remains in real use (synthetic probes only); Individual tolerance of the regain after a gap, and how common the D57 configuration is.
No ASK, HOLD or clinical routing is needed for these nonclinical readings; clinical pauses route as before.

sources.title: The Duration of the Repeated-Bout Effect After Eccentric Exercise
sources.authors: Theodorou AA, Margaritelis NV, Karyofyllidou AV, Christodoulou F, Jamurtas AZ, et al.
sources.population_design_dose: 48 young recreationally active men; two identical bouts of maximal eccentric knee-extensor exercise (5 x 15 repetitions); after the first bout participants were randomly allocated to repeat it after 3, 6, 9 or 12 weeks (12 completers per group).
sources.findings: The repeated-bout effect (smaller losses of torque and range of motion, less soreness and muscle damage) was evident at 3 and 6 weeks for most outcomes, remained detectable at 9 weeks for selected markers, and was no longer meaningfully present at 12 weeks.
sources.locator: Abstract; Methods 2.2 (random allocation to the interval groups); Results (Table 2, model-estimated contrasts by interval); Discussion (earlier downhill-running and elbow-flexor studies); Limitations (ssctr-evidence/PMC13674372.xml).
limitations: Maximal unaccustomed eccentric knee-extensor work in young men; resistance training at 2-3 reps in reserve damages muscle far less; markers assessed on days 2 and 4 only; activity between bouts not monitored.
counterevidence: Earlier studies cited in the discussion found protection that faded by 9 weeks after downhill running and persisted partly to 10 weeks for the elbow flexors.

sources.title: American College of Sports Medicine Position Stand. Resistance Training Prescription for Muscle Function, Hypertrophy, and Physical Performance in Healthy Adults: An Overview of Reviews
sources.authors: Currier BS, D'Souza AC, Singh MAF, Lowisz CV, Rawson ES, Schoenfeld BJ, Smith-Ryan AE, et al.
sources.population_design_dose: Overview of 137 systematic reviews of randomized trials in healthy adults (>=18 y), resistance training >=6 wk; most evidence from novice trainees.
sources.findings: Resistance training improves strength and hypertrophy versus control; strength enhanced by heavier loads, 2-3 sets, >=2 sessions/wk and exercise at session start; hypertrophy by >=10 sets/muscle/wk; training to failure and periodization not consistently influential; perceived-exertion scales can raise absolute load with strength gains; individualization encouraged for adherence.
sources.locator: Abstract; Results (strength, hypertrophy); Discussion subsections Progressive overload, Specificity/Individualization, Variation.
limitations: Overview of reviews dominated by novice trainees; not concurrent-training or runner specific.
No per-session increment, establishment or return procedure is specified.
counterevidence: States progression is not always necessary for benefit, so planned progression is a choice, not a requirement.

sources.title: Detraining and tapering effects on hormonal responses and strength performance
sources.authors: Izquierdo M, Ibanez J, Gonzalez-Badillo JJ, Ratamess NA, Kraemer WJ, Hakkinen K, et al.
sources.population_design_dose: 46 physically active men matched and randomly assigned, after 16 weeks of periodized heavy resistance training, to 4 weeks of complete cessation (n = 14), a taper (n = 11) or continued training (n = 21).
sources.findings: Four weeks of cessation decreased maximal strength by 6-9% and muscle power by 14-17% in arm and leg extensors; the taper gave a further 2% strength gain.
limitations: Abstract only; men only; strength-trained; 4 weeks of complete cessation, not a reduced or time-trimmed dose.
counterevidence: Losses within four weeks are moderate, so a short gap is not neutral but does not by itself call for a long rebuild.

sources.title: Skeletal muscle adaptations to physical inactivity and subsequent retraining in young men
sources.authors: Campbell EL, Seynnes OR, Bottinelli R, McPhee JS, Atherton PJ, Jones DA, Butler-Browne G, Narici MV
sources.population_design_dose: 8 young men; 3 weeks of unilateral lower-limb suspension, then a 3-week resistance-training recovery programme; no control group.
sources.findings: Isometric torque fell 26% and quadriceps volume 10% after 3 weeks of unloading; all measures were restored to pre-suspension values after 3 weeks of retraining.
limitations: Abstract only; unloading model, not detraining; 8 men; no control group; retraining dose not stated in the abstract.
counterevidence: Fast restoration after disuse does not show that a sudden volume increase is free of soreness or damage.

sources.title: The Importance of Recovery in Resistance Training Microcycle Construction
sources.authors: Sousa CA, Zourdos MC, Storey AG, Helms ER
sources.population_design_dose: Review of 24 studies of recovery between resistance-training sessions (PubMed, Medline, SPORTDiscus, Scopus, CINAHL).
sources.findings: Higher volumes may increase recovery demands; with wide individual variation the authors suggest starting with lower volume, monitoring recovery and increasing volume gradually; lower-body, multi-joint, eccentric and lengthened-position exercises may need longer recovery.
sources.locator: Abstract (PubMed efetch, reviews/ssctr-r7a1-abstracts.out.txt); PMCID PMC11057610 not read.
limitations: Abstract only; narrative synthesis of heterogeneous studies; not about returns after a gap.
counterevidence: Supports a gradual reintroduction of accessory volume, the R23 policy question, without giving a rule or a threshold.

claims.statement: D53’s class is a set count the declared policy places under a restoration ceiling (a regain cap after a re-establishment; the return steps, cap and ceiling after a return) coming back faster than that ceiling allows, in any state mode or handler path. The R23 exercises are under no such ceiling in the declared policy, so no ceiling is reset or bypassed; covering them needs a new sporting rule, which this mission forbids.
claims.applicability: The D53 closure criterion of Founder §10.
limitations: A scope reading of declared rules and my earlier records, not a scientific claim.
counterevidence: The jump has the same shape (1 to 3 sets when time returns) as the capped D56 and D57 cases.

claims.statement: The magnitude is small: bodyweight rows, or effort-chosen loads at RIR 3 or more, up to 3 sets; repeated-bout protection persists for weeks (R6-S48), 2-3 sets per exercise is the position stand’s range for strength (R6-S01), four weeks of cessation cost 6-9% strength (R7A1-S01) and three weeks of retraining restored unloading losses (R7A1-S02).
claims.applicability: Accessories outside any ceiling after gaps of up to five weeks.
limitations: R7A1-S01 and R7A1-S02 are abstract-only; no study of accessory volume after a return.
counterevidence: A review advises starting with lower volume and increasing gradually (R7A1-S03), which favours the R23 policy question rather than a jump.

claims.statement: No source supports a specific ceiling for uncovered accessories; I abstain on such a rule and keep R23 for the next policy revision.
limitations: Abstract-level counterevidence only.
counterevidence: R7A1-S03 (gradual increase).

sources.title: American College of Sports Medicine Position Stand. Resistance Training Prescription for Muscle Function, Hypertrophy, and Physical Performance in Healthy Adults: An Overview of Reviews
sources.authors: Currier BS, D'Souza AC, Singh MAF, Lowisz CV, Rawson ES, Schoenfeld BJ, Smith-Ryan AE, et al.
sources.population_design_dose: Overview of 137 systematic reviews of randomized trials in healthy adults (>=18 y), resistance training >=6 wk; most evidence from novice trainees.
sources.findings: Resistance training improves strength and hypertrophy versus control; strength enhanced by heavier loads, 2-3 sets, >=2 sessions/wk and exercise at session start; hypertrophy by >=10 sets/muscle/wk; training to failure and periodization not consistently influential; perceived-exertion scales can raise absolute load with strength gains; individualization encouraged for adherence.
sources.locator: Abstract; Results (strength, hypertrophy); Discussion subsections Progressive overload, Specificity/Individualization, Variation.
limitations: Overview of reviews dominated by novice trainees; not concurrent-training or runner specific.
No per-session increment, establishment or return procedure is specified.
counterevidence: States progression is not always necessary for benefit, so planned progression is a choice, not a requirement.

sources.title: Detraining: loss of training-induced physiological and performance adaptations. Part I: short term insufficient training stimulus
sources.authors: Mujika I, Padilla S
sources.population_design_dose: Narrative review of short-term detraining (less than 4 weeks of insufficient training stimulus) in athletes and recently trained individuals.
sources.findings: Short-term cardiorespiratory detraining in highly trained athletes brings a rapid decline in VO2max and blood volume and impaired endurance performance; the changes are more moderate in recently trained individuals; strength declines are limited.
limitations: Narrative review, abstract only; highly trained athletes; no dose rule for the first session back.
counterevidence: Declines are described as rapid in highly trained athletes, so a short break is not free of loss.

sources.title: Effect of short-term training cessation on performance measures in distance runners
sources.authors: Houmard JA, Hortobagyi T, Johns RA, Bruno NJ, Nute CC, Shinebarger MH, Welborn JW
sources.population_design_dose: 12 distance runners; 14 days of training cessation; measures before and after, no control group.
sources.findings: VO2max fell about 4% (61.6 to 58.7 ml/kg/min), time to exhaustion about 9% and submaximal heart rate rose about 6%; running economy did not change; the authors call the VO2max reduction relatively small.
limitations: Abstract only; small uncontrolled sample; 14 days, longer than the short return class.
counterevidence: Time to exhaustion fell more than VO2max, so performance may drop more than VO2max suggests.

sources.title: Two weeks of detraining reduces cardiopulmonary function and muscular fitness in endurance athletes
sources.authors: Chen YT, Hsieh YY, Ho JY, Lin TY, Lin JC
sources.population_design_dose: 15 endurance-trained men aged 19-26; 2 weeks of detraining; measures before and after.
sources.findings: VO2max, time to exhaustion, maximal stroke volume and knee-extensor strength fell significantly after two weeks; muscle endurance was maintained.
limitations: Abstract only; small uncontrolled sample of young men; two weeks, longer than the short return class.
counterevidence: A measurable loss within two weeks argues against treating a short break as no break.

sources.title: Cardiac size and VO2max do not decrease after short-term exercise cessation
sources.authors: Cullinane EM, Sady SP, Vadeboncoeur L, Burke M, Thompson PD
sources.population_design_dose: 15 male competitive distance runners (28 years); 10 days of exercise cessation after 2 weeks of 16 km daily; controlled diet.
sources.findings: Estimated plasma volume fell about 5% and peak exercise heart rate rose about 5%; VO2max, resting heart rate, blood pressure and cardiac dimensions did not change.
limitations: Abstract only; small uncontrolled sample; men only; 1986.
counterevidence: Plasma volume and peak heart rate changed within 10 days.

claims.statement: A never-performed substitute is established by effort at a low volume (at most 2 sets at RIR 3 or more, no load converted), consistent with the position stand’s low starting volume and effort-adjusted load (R6-S01); prescribing it for a session still ahead the same day replaces a session the athlete cannot do.
claims.applicability: Same-day equipment changes.
limitations: Position-stand evidence is mostly from novices.
counterevidence: None located.

claims.statement: After at most 10 days without running VO2max was unchanged in distance runners (R7A-S06) and fell about 4% after 14 days (R7A-S04); two weeks of detraining reduced VO2max and strength (R7A-S05); short-term detraining is rapid in highly trained athletes (R7A-S03). The easy first quality slot is a declared conservative step (condition 7); missing it leaves the first quality session at the resumed dose, and after a 10-day break at an earned step above the last executed one (D58).
claims.applicability: Short returns (at most return.shortMaxDays days).
limitations: Abstracts only; small uncontrolled samples, mostly trained men.
counterevidence: In the D58 configuration the athlete has run two or more sessions after the break before the quality session.

claims.statement: C1 is a reading of time, not physiology: a session that may already have been done is never rewritten, and a session still to come gets the return rule; noon as the end of a morning shift is an operational convention of a plan that knows only the shift.
claims.applicability: Every handler’s same-day reading.
limitations: The plan cannot see the athlete’s clock.
counterevidence: An athlete who trains at 11:00 and reports at 11:30 sees that morning’s session re-planned before the report arrives.

records.applicability: Runtime compositions and readings of declared rules inside the approved envelopes, offline synthetic Node24 reference, stated adult recreational nonclinical V1 population; no real-athlete effect.

decision.rationale: R7ASM-SSCTR-r1 delta check: carries: outside the delta; short, same-day and x-sameday grids byte-identical. R7ASE-SSCTR-r1 delta check: carries: outside the delta; short and same-day grids byte-identical. R7AB-SSCTR-r1 delta check: carries: outside the delta; short and same-day grids byte-identical. R7AF-SSCTR-r1 delta check: carries: outside the delta; short grid byte-identical. R7A2-SSCTR-r1 rationale: R7A2-SSCTR-r1 delta check: carries with D58 met and C1 applied by every same-day handler; unchanged by the R7-A.2 delta. R7A1-SSCTR-r2 rationale: R7A1-SSCTR-r2 delta check: carries with D58 now met and C1 applied by every same-day handler. R7A1-SSCTR-r1 rationale: C1 gives every handler one reading of "still ahead", and the noon end of a morning shift is an acceptable operational convention: on both sides of it the dose stays at or below the last executed dose and a session that may have been done is never rewritten. The same-day morning case of QE-R7A-02 is fixed. Condition 7 is not met when re-entry starts in the return’s week but that week’s quality slot is already past: the first quality slot after the break is next week’s and it keeps its quality dose, after a 10-day break one earned step above the last executed quality (D58, blocking: the same class as QE-R7A-02). The same-day substitution and the evening return raise no sporting objection.
preserve: One test of "still ahead" for every handler
History is never rewritten
The easy slot is an adaptation of its week and survives re-plans
decision.mec_change_level: No policy change; one blocking runtime change (D58).
decision.trade_off: One easy session after a short break, against keeping the athlete’s quality rhythm; nothing else changes.
must_not: Present any value as validated physiology, an injury-prevention threshold, a readiness score or a guarantee.
Substitute a training dose for clinical assessment.
Treat missing data as adverse or as tolerance.
Change official plan state or completed history.

The start state of a return is the state at its interruption under R7A2-SSCTR-INTERRUPTION-STATE (revision R7ASM-SSCTR-r1), INTERRUPTION_EPISODE_CONTRACT R7AF-INTERRUPTION-1, WEEK_START_AUTHORITY_CONTRACT R7AB-WEEKSTART-1 (its record, temporal-contradiction rule and boundaries B1-B7, B9-B11) and STATE_MODEL_CONTRACT R7ASM-STATE-MODEL-1 (which replaces STATE_EVIDENCE_CONTRACT R7ASE-STATE-EVIDENCE-1): a correction names its interruption (episodeId) or repeats its days and starts from what the athlete had executed at its own start; a break after a re-entry or after training is new and starts from that re-entry plus the facts executed since; the state at the interruption is read value by value (one value per strength exercise, one for the run): a stored value counts only when its start holds that value as evidence decided before the cut (the intake, a return’s entry, the weekly review’s rule on that value’s historical value, or a projection whose own base value was historical and that the week before executed per sport exactly as assumed, loads included); a value a review carried from a projection is rebuilt by the review’s rule on its historical value; otherwise the value moves back to its last such start and the sessions executed after it are facts only (a known load lifted is the load under D44; a projected dose lifted is that load with its repetition target, never a load tick only the projection counted); weeks never reported are not history; a named correction that contradicts its own executed re-entry is asked; anything else is asked; each short break owns its easy slot.

Weekly-review contract: these bindings hold when every elapsed week receives a gating weekly review, in order and after its last session, with unreported sessions reviewed as missed. A week that receives no gating review keeps the projection's assumption that it was executed and logged (establishment, progression, block credit, achieved peaks and the strength resume clock); that path is outside this approval and must be closed before any use beyond the offline reference (R18).

sources.title: American College of Sports Medicine Position Stand. Resistance Training Prescription for Muscle Function, Hypertrophy, and Physical Performance in Healthy Adults: An Overview of Reviews
sources.authors: Currier BS, D'Souza AC, Singh MAF, Lowisz CV, Rawson ES, Schoenfeld BJ, Smith-Ryan AE, et al.
sources.population_design_dose: Overview of 137 systematic reviews of randomized trials in healthy adults (>=18 y), resistance training >=6 wk; most evidence from novice trainees.
sources.findings: Resistance training improves strength and hypertrophy versus control; strength enhanced by heavier loads, 2-3 sets, >=2 sessions/wk and exercise at session start; hypertrophy by >=10 sets/muscle/wk; training to failure and periodization not consistently influential; perceived-exertion scales can raise absolute load with strength gains; individualization encouraged for adherence.
sources.locator: Abstract; Results (strength, hypertrophy); Discussion subsections Progressive overload, Specificity/Individualization, Variation.
limitations: Overview of reviews dominated by novice trainees; not concurrent-training or runner specific.
No per-session increment, establishment or return procedure is specified.
counterevidence: States progression is not always necessary for benefit, so planned progression is a choice, not a requirement.

sources.title: The Effect of Load and Volume Autoregulation on Muscular Strength and Hypertrophy: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
sources.authors: Hickmott LM, Chilibeck PD, Shaw KA, Butcher SJ
sources.population_design_dose: 15 studies in resistance-trained individuals: six on load autoregulation (RIR-based RPE, velocity) against percentage-based loading, nine on volume autoregulation by velocity-loss thresholds.
sources.findings: Autoregulated and standardized load prescription gave similar 1RM gains (MD 2.07 kg, 95% CI -0.32 to 4.46); velocity-loss thresholds of 25% or less favoured strength and higher thresholds hypertrophy.
sources.locator: Abstract (PubMed efetch, reviews/ssctr-r7a1-abstracts.out.txt); PMCID PMC8762534 not read.
limitations: Abstract only; trained individuals; no study of logged-load adoption or of a lighter load chosen by the athlete.
counterevidence: Similar mean gains do not show that adopting a lighter self-chosen load is neutral for every athlete.

claims.statement: Resistance-training prescription is a repetition range per goal with load adjusted to effort (R6-S01); keeping the planned target on HOLD and REGRESS at the adopted lighter load keeps the prescription inside the range, while letting the short set become the target walked it below the range (3x2 and 3x3 for 4-6) with no evidence of benefit.
claims.applicability: Known-load rows logged at a lighter load.
limitations: Position-stand ranges are group-level guidance; the gates are declared operational rules.
counterevidence: Repeated misses at the lighter load still regress one step at a time, which may be slower than an athlete needs.

claims.statement: Effort-based (RIR) load selection gives strength gains similar to percentage-based loading in trained individuals (R7A1-S04), consistent with adopting the athlete’s effort-chosen lighter load as the reference.
claims.applicability: Background for the adoption of a lighter load.
limitations: Abstract only; no study of logged-load adoption.
counterevidence: A lighter load chosen for reasons other than capacity lowers the stimulus.

records.applicability: Runtime compositions and readings of declared rules inside the approved envelopes, offline synthetic Node24 reference, stated adult recreational nonclinical V1 population; no real-athlete effect.

decision.rationale: R7ASM-SSCTR-r1 delta check: does not carry: condition 2 (HOLD and REGRESS keep the planned repetition target) is not met on the R42 path. F2 (ssctr-r7asm-reps-probe.mjs, STRENGTH goal range [4,6]): the projected 82.5 kg lifted for 3 of 5 repetitions at the prescribed reserve (HOLD) in a reviewed week gives ["2026-12-02 3x3@3 KNOWN 82.5 KNOWN","2026-12-09 3x3@3 KNOWN 82.5 KNOWN","2026-12-16 3x3@3 KNOWN 85 KNOWN","2026-12-23 2x3@3 KNOWN 85 KNOWN"] (outside the range: 4 rows); the predecessor ["2026-12-02 3x5@3 KNOWN 82.5 KNOWN","2026-12-09 3x5@3 KNOWN 85 KNOWN","2026-12-16 3x5@3 KNOWN 85 KNOWN","2026-12-23 2x5@3 KNOWN 87.5 KNOWN"]. Eight repetitions at reserve 0 (HOLD) give ["2026-12-02 3x6@3 KNOWN 82.5 KNOWN","2026-12-09 3x6@3 KNOWN 82.5 KNOWN","2026-12-16 3x6@3 KNOWN 85 KNOWN","2026-12-23 2x6@3 KNOWN 85 KNOWN"]; the predecessor ["2026-12-02 3x5@3 KNOWN 82.5 KNOWN","2026-12-09 3x5@3 KNOWN 85 KNOWN","2026-12-16 3x5@3 KNOWN 85 KNOWN","2026-12-23 2x5@3 KNOWN 87.5 KNOWN"]. Same class in my tick probe (missed/missed: 3x3 and 4x3 at 22-26 kg on both U and R). earnedAt sets the repetitions logged whatever the gate, before advanceStrength's HOLD rule keeps "the planned target". This reintroduces the defect DR-1 named (a short set walked the target below the range: 3x2 and 3x3 for 4-6). R7ASE-SSCTR-r1 delta check: carries; history now reads a logged load by the same adoption rule the review uses. R7AB-SSCTR-r1 delta check: carries unchanged. R7AF-SSCTR-r1 delta check: carries unchanged. R7A2-SSCTR-r1 rationale: R7A2-SSCTR-r1 delta check: carries unchanged. R7A1-SSCTR-r2 rationale: R7A1-SSCTR-r2 delta check: carries unchanged. R7A1-SSCTR-r1 rationale: The reading separates observation, progression evidence and target as the Founder asks: a logged load against a known-load exposure is progression evidence, so the declared gate decides the target, and only an establishment exposure sets its target from what it logged. HOLD then repeats the planned target at the adopted lighter load, which keeps the prescription inside the goal’s range and never above the planned dose; ADVANCE behaves as at the planned load. My R25 ("keep or clamp the target") is met.
