A logged load of an exposure that prescribed a known load is progression evidence: HOLD and REGRESS keep the planned repetition target (REGRESS lowers the load one smallest increment, or the repetitions by repStep down to the range floor when no load is known); ADVANCE or EARNED takes the logged repetitions as at the planned load, the prescription staying inside the goal’s range (met).
A lighter logged load is adopted only under the existing adoption rules, never above a re-establishment ceiling; a heavier one only when that exposure met the ADVANCE criterion (D44, D45) (met).
Only an establishment exposure (first establishment, re-establishment, return entry, from-log) sets its target from its logged repetitions (met).

D59 (met at R7A2-FREEZE-1 and at R7A-FINAL-FREEZE and at R7A-BOUNDARY-FINAL-FREEZE and at STATE-EVIDENCE-FREEZE-1 and at HISTORICAL-PROJECTION-FREEZE-1, closed): a return starts from the state at the break (stateAtBreak, strengthAtBreak): every exercise executed before the break’s first day is in use with its last performed date and, outside a return step and a phase reduction, its last executed whole count after the time fit (target met) as the ceiling (the largest of the break week, R20); a moderate or long return enters it at strengthEntrySets with strengthEntryMinimumRir or more, step 2 follows, the block in progress earns no set and the count comes back at most one set per executed whole week up to the ceiling; the progression the pre-break exposures earned stays unapplied. Regression: ssctr-r7a1-recheck-firstweek.mjs with E, O and B at 0 for NONE and FAMILIAR and O at 0 for KNOWN, my restoration, cap and short grids, and test "R7-A.2 I4/I5/I8 (SSCTR D59)". R7ASE-SSCTR-r1: the state at the break also takes the load the athlete lifted on a known-load row as the exercise’s load (lighter, or heavier only under D44: at most one smallest increment above the row and the row’s target met), a fact and never a step; an effort-guided row adopts nothing; a projected dose lifted exactly is that load with its repetition target and no further step. This approval excludes a stored load tick that counts an exposure the projection assumed and the athlete did not execute (NF-R7ASE-3, R42).

The start state of a return is the state at its interruption under R7A2-SSCTR-INTERRUPTION-STATE (revision R7ASM-SSCTR-r1), INTERRUPTION_EPISODE_CONTRACT R7AF-INTERRUPTION-1, WEEK_START_AUTHORITY_CONTRACT R7AB-WEEKSTART-1 (its record, temporal-contradiction rule and boundaries B1-B7, B9-B11) and STATE_MODEL_CONTRACT R7ASM-STATE-MODEL-1 (which replaces STATE_EVIDENCE_CONTRACT R7ASE-STATE-EVIDENCE-1): a correction names its interruption (episodeId) or repeats its days and starts from what the athlete had executed at its own start; a break after a re-entry or after training is new and starts from that re-entry plus the facts executed since; the state at the interruption is read value by value (one value per strength exercise, one for the run): a stored value counts only when its start holds that value as evidence decided before the cut (the intake, a return’s entry, the weekly review’s rule on that value’s historical value, or a projection whose own base value was historical and that the week before executed per sport exactly as assumed, loads included); a value a review carried from a projection is rebuilt by the review’s rule on its historical value; otherwise the value moves back to its last such start and the sessions executed after it are facts only (a known load lifted is the load under D44; a projected dose lifted is that load with its repetition target, never a load tick only the projection counted); weeks never reported are not history; a named correction that contradicts its own executed re-entry is asked; anything else is asked; each short break owns its easy slot.

Weekly-review contract: these bindings hold when every elapsed week receives a gating weekly review, in order and after its last session, with unreported sessions reviewed as missed. A week that receives no gating review keeps the projection's assumption that it was executed and logged (establishment, progression, block credit, achieved peaks and the strength resume clock); that path is outside this approval and must be closed before any use beyond the offline reference (R18).

sources.title: Effects of tapering on performance in endurance athletes: A systematic review and meta-analysis
sources.authors: Wang Z, Wang YT, Gao W, Zhong Y
sources.population_design_dose: 14 studies in well-trained endurance athletes (VO2max >55 ml/kg/min).
sources.findings: Taper improved time-trial (SMD -0.45) and time-to-exhaustion performance; volume reductions of 41-60% with maintained intensity and frequency, durations <=7, 8-14 or 15-21 days and progressive or step tapers were effective.
limitations: Trained, not recreational, athletes; few studies per subgroup.
counterevidence: No change in VO2max or economy; benefits depend on prior overload.

sources.title: The Duration of the Repeated-Bout Effect After Eccentric Exercise
sources.authors: Theodorou AA, Margaritelis NV, Karyofyllidou AV, Christodoulou F, Jamurtas AZ, et al.
sources.population_design_dose: 48 young recreationally active men; two identical bouts of maximal eccentric knee-extensor exercise (5 x 15 repetitions); after the first bout participants were randomly allocated to repeat it after 3, 6, 9 or 12 weeks (12 completers per group).
sources.findings: The repeated-bout effect (smaller losses of torque and range of motion, less soreness and muscle damage) was evident at 3 and 6 weeks for most outcomes, remained detectable at 9 weeks for selected markers, and was no longer meaningfully present at 12 weeks.
sources.locator: Abstract; Methods 2.2 (random allocation to the interval groups); Results (Table 2, model-estimated contrasts by interval); Discussion (earlier downhill-running and elbow-flexor studies); Limitations (ssctr-evidence/PMC13674372.xml).
limitations: Maximal unaccustomed eccentric knee-extensor work in young men; resistance training at 2-3 reps in reserve damages muscle far less; markers assessed on days 2 and 4 only; activity between bouts not monitored.
counterevidence: Earlier studies cited in the discussion found protection that faded by 9 weeks after downhill running and persisted partly to 10 weeks for the elbow flexors.

sources.title: American College of Sports Medicine Position Stand. Resistance Training Prescription for Muscle Function, Hypertrophy, and Physical Performance in Healthy Adults: An Overview of Reviews
sources.authors: Currier BS, D'Souza AC, Singh MAF, Lowisz CV, Rawson ES, Schoenfeld BJ, Smith-Ryan AE, et al.
sources.population_design_dose: Overview of 137 systematic reviews of randomized trials in healthy adults (>=18 y), resistance training >=6 wk; most evidence from novice trainees.
sources.findings: Resistance training improves strength and hypertrophy versus control; strength enhanced by heavier loads, 2-3 sets, >=2 sessions/wk and exercise at session start; hypertrophy by >=10 sets/muscle/wk; training to failure and periodization not consistently influential; perceived-exertion scales can raise absolute load with strength gains; individualization encouraged for adherence.
sources.locator: Abstract; Results (strength, hypertrophy); Discussion subsections Progressive overload, Specificity/Individualization, Variation.
limitations: Overview of reviews dominated by novice trainees; not concurrent-training or runner specific.
No per-session increment, establishment or return procedure is specified.
counterevidence: States progression is not always necessary for benefit, so planned progression is a choice, not a requirement.

sources.title: Acute Neuromuscular, Physiological and Performance Responses After Strength Training in Runners: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
sources.authors: de Carvalho e Silva GI, Brandao LHA, dos Santos Silva D, de Jesus Alves MD, Aidar FJ, et al.
sources.population_design_dose: 19 studies (13 meta-analysed) of male runners; one strength session (traditional, explosive, plyometric or combined) before running tests, mostly 24-48 h later.
sources.findings: After a strength session peak torque fell and soreness, creatine kinase and perceived exertion rose; jump height, ventilation, oxygen uptake, lactate and heart rate were not different, and submaximal running was little affected; time to exhaustion fell in three of the four studies that measured it. The authors advise care to limit muscle damage before competition.
sources.locator: Abstract; Key Points; Results (time to exhaustion in four studies); Discussion; Practical Implications (ssctr-evidence/PMC9385928.xml).
limitations: Male participants only; small heterogeneous studies, several with damaging or 6RM protocols; no study of a taper or of a low-dose session.
counterevidence: Submaximal running physiology at 24 h was largely unchanged after strength sessions, even after damaging protocols.

sources.title: Gaining more from doing less? The effects of a one-week deload period during supervised resistance training on muscular adaptations
sources.authors: Coleman M, Burke R, Augustin F, Pinero A, Maldonado J, Fisher JP, Israetel M, et al.
sources.population_design_dose: 39 resistance-trained young men and women; 9-week high-volume program; one group abstained from training for 1 week at the midpoint and then resumed the same program, the other trained continuously.
sources.findings: No appreciable between-group differences in lower-body muscle size, local endurance or power; the continuous group improved isometric and dynamic lower-body strength more than the deload group.
sources.locator: Abstract; Methods (group allocation, deload at the midpoint); Results; Limitations (ssctr-evidence/PMC10809978.xml).
limitations: The deload was complete cessation, not a set reduction; resistance-trained young adults; upper-body training unsupervised.
counterevidence: Strength gains were smaller after one week without training, so breaks are not neutral for strength.

claims.statement: Effective endurance tapers last up to about three weeks with 41-60% less volume and kept intensity (R6-S14); a taper of a superseded date five weeks before the new race is not a taper of that race, so returning the remaining days to the build dose, as a program generated with the new date would, keeps training while one taper precedes the race.
claims.applicability: Event changes that move remaining days out of the event window.
limitations: Trained endurance athletes in R6-S14.
counterevidence: The athlete loses two or three days of the reduced load already begun; no detraining is expected over that span.

claims.statement: Repeated-bout protection fades over weeks (R6-S48) and low-volume effort-guided entries are consistent with the position stand (R6-S01); a lift not performed since a break therefore starts at the entry dose, never at a later return step without an entry, and a session of the plan before the break neither moves into the re-entry nor counts as done.
claims.applicability: Returns reported mid-week.
limitations: Maximal eccentric work in R6-S48; novices in R6-S01.
counterevidence: None located.

claims.statement: Holding next week’s step after a converging systemic fatigue signal is conservative and cheap (R6-S53, R6-S45), so a recorded signal must survive a later review of the same week.
claims.applicability: Late-week fatigue reports.
limitations: Male runners (R6-S53); trained young adults (R6-S45).
counterevidence: None located.

claims.statement: A conditional start is planning, not prediction: rows are assumed executed as every later week is planned, and the weekly review re-derives the start from evidence; the single-run ceiling reading of planned weeks is the policy text.
claims.applicability: Mid-week changes to future weeks.
limitations: Rests on the weekly-review contract (R18).
counterevidence: A week that never receives its review keeps the assumption (R18, outside approval).

claims.statement: No study tests the order effects of same-week adaptations; the compositions are declared readings.
limitations: None searched beyond Q1 and Q2.
counterevidence: None located.

records.applicability: Runtime compositions and readings of declared rules inside the approved envelopes, offline synthetic Node24 reference, stated adult recreational nonclinical V1 population; no real-athlete effect.

S5 (C5): a session dated before a return reported the same week is never moved into the re-entry and never counts as done in next week’s conditional plan; a lift not done since the break starts at the return entry (strengthEntrySets at RIR at least strengthEntryMinimumRir), never at a later step without an entry; a newer report of a break that began this week starts from the start the week had before an earlier report of it, so a corrected report plans the week as the corrected report alone (met).

S6 (C3): once the week is complete, its evidence decides next week’s start whatever handler re-plans (an unreported complete week holds); while the week is under way, the conditional plan of the week as now planned decides, its rows assumed executed as prescribed except sessions dated before a return; a return’s re-base of next week is kept; the weekly review re-derives the start from evidence (met).

S6 (run ceiling): in a conditional projection the earlier projected weeks count as executed for the single-run ceiling, as the policy states; the first week a review projects uses completed runs only (met).

S9 (C5): an event change re-plans this week’s remaining days when it moves one of them into or out of the taper, race-window or post-event days, by days to the race; completed sessions stay as executed; only the taper of the event in force remains; the race statement stays the longest continuous run planned before the race (met).

S10 (C4): content an adaptation moves into a slot keeps the week’s earlier adaptations, each with its own clock; a move never uses a skipped slot; a systemic fatigue report with nothing left to reduce reviews the week with its signal and records it, so a later review of the same week keeps it; a mid-week reduction does not set that signal (met).

S10 (C2): a change stated from a later date applies from the first week that begins on or after it, starting that week from the week before it as planned with its transition under the new context (met).

S8: the first strength week after a break stays RETURN_ENTRY with the run in RETURN mode whatever change of the same evening comes first; a moved race leaves one race; a reviewed transition survives a later equipment change; same-week adaptations survive an event change (met).

D59 (met at R7A2-FREEZE-1 and at R7A-FINAL-FREEZE and at R7A-BOUNDARY-FINAL-FREEZE and at STATE-EVIDENCE-FREEZE-1 and at HISTORICAL-PROJECTION-FREEZE-1, closed): a return starts from the state at the break (stateAtBreak, strengthAtBreak): every exercise executed before the break’s first day is in use with its last performed date and, outside a return step and a phase reduction, its last executed whole count after the time fit (target met) as the ceiling (the largest of the break week, R20); a moderate or long return enters it at strengthEntrySets with strengthEntryMinimumRir or more, step 2 follows, the block in progress earns no set and the count comes back at most one set per executed whole week up to the ceiling; the progression the pre-break exposures earned stays unapplied. This approval excludes a stored load tick that counts an exposure the projection assumed and the athlete did not execute (NF-R7ASE-3, R42).

The start state of a return is the state at its interruption under R7A2-SSCTR-INTERRUPTION-STATE (revision R7ASM-SSCTR-r1), INTERRUPTION_EPISODE_CONTRACT R7AF-INTERRUPTION-1, WEEK_START_AUTHORITY_CONTRACT R7AB-WEEKSTART-1 (its record, temporal-contradiction rule and boundaries B1-B7, B9-B11) and STATE_MODEL_CONTRACT R7ASM-STATE-MODEL-1 (which replaces STATE_EVIDENCE_CONTRACT R7ASE-STATE-EVIDENCE-1): a correction names its interruption (episodeId) or repeats its days and starts from what the athlete had executed at its own start; a break after a re-entry or after training is new and starts from that re-entry plus the facts executed since; the state at the interruption is read value by value (one value per strength exercise, one for the run): a stored value counts only when its start holds that value as evidence decided before the cut (the intake, a return’s entry, the weekly review’s rule on that value’s historical value, or a projection whose own base value was historical and that the week before executed per sport exactly as assumed, loads included); a value a review carried from a projection is rebuilt by the review’s rule on its historical value; otherwise the value moves back to its last such start and the sessions executed after it are facts only (a known load lifted is the load under D44; a projected dose lifted is that load with its repetition target, never a load tick only the projection counted); weeks never reported are not history; a named correction that contradicts its own executed re-entry is asked; anything else is asked; each short break owns its easy slot.

Weekly-review contract: these bindings hold when every elapsed week receives a gating weekly review, in order and after its last session, with unreported sessions reviewed as missed. sources.title: The Duration of the Repeated-Bout Effect After Eccentric Exercise
sources.authors: Theodorou AA, Margaritelis NV, Karyofyllidou AV, Christodoulou F, Jamurtas AZ, et al.
sources.population_design_dose: 48 young recreationally active men; two identical bouts of maximal eccentric knee-extensor exercise (5 x 15 repetitions); after the first bout participants were randomly allocated to repeat it after 3, 6, 9 or 12 weeks (12 completers per group).
sources.findings: The repeated-bout effect (smaller losses of torque and range of motion, less soreness and muscle damage) was evident at 3 and 6 weeks for most outcomes, remained detectable at 9 weeks for selected markers, and was no longer meaningfully present at 12 weeks.
sources.locator: Abstract; Methods 2.2 (random allocation to the interval groups); Results (Table 2, model-estimated contrasts by interval); Discussion (earlier downhill-running and elbow-flexor studies); Limitations (ssctr-evidence/PMC13674372.xml).
limitations: Maximal unaccustomed eccentric knee-extensor work in young men; resistance training at 2-3 reps in reserve damages muscle far less; markers assessed on days 2 and 4 only; activity between bouts not monitored.
counterevidence: Earlier studies cited in the discussion found protection that faded by 9 weeks after downhill running and persisted partly to 10 weeks for the elbow flexors.

sources.title: Low-intensity eccentric contractions of the knee extensors and flexors protect against muscle damage
sources.authors: Lin MJ, Chen TC, Chen HL, Wu BH, Nosaka K
sources.population_design_dose: Young men in 8 experimental and 2 control groups (13 per group); 30 or 60 low-intensity eccentric contractions (10% of maximal isometric strength) of the knee flexors or extensors 2 days, 1, 2 or 3 weeks before maximal eccentric contractions of the same muscles.
sources.findings: The low-intensity bout caused no measurable damage itself and gave 30-66% protection against damage from the maximal bout when it came 2 days or 1 week before; there was no protection at 2 or 3 weeks.
limitations: Abstract only; maximal isokinetic eccentric contractions damage muscle far more than effort-guided training at 3 reps in reserve; young men only.
counterevidence: The protective window of a low-dose bout was about one week, shorter than after a damaging bout (R6-S48).

sources.title: Damage protective effects conferred by low-intensity eccentric contractions on arm, leg and trunk muscles
sources.authors: Huang MJ, Nosaka K, Wang HS, Tseng KW, Chen HL, Chou TY, Chen TC
sources.population_design_dose: 24 untrained young men (12 per group); 50 eccentric contractions at 10% of maximal isometric strength 2 days before 50 at 80%, for nine muscle groups, against a group without the low-intensity bout.
sources.findings: With the low-intensity bout 2 days before, strength recovered faster (6-31% greater at 5 days) and peak soreness was 36-54% lower after the high-intensity bout, in all nine muscle groups.
limitations: Abstract only; the allocation method is not stated in the abstract; eccentric-only protocols in untrained young men.
counterevidence: The size of the protection differed between muscles.

sources.title: Comparative effects of single vs. multiple-set resistance training on neuromuscular performance and muscle morphology in sedentary men
sources.authors: Coskun IA, Kafkas ME
sources.population_design_dose: 34 sedentary young men randomized (computer-generated sequence, sealed opaque envelopes) to single-set, three-set or control; 8 weeks, twice weekly, seven exercises of up to 10 repetitions.
sources.findings: Both single-set and three-set training improved strength, power and muscle size over 8 weeks; three sets gave larger gains (squat 1-RM +14.8% and leg cross-sectional area +11.3%, against about 6-8% with one set), a volume dose-response from the first weeks.
sources.locator: Abstract; Methods (randomization, concealed allocation, training programme); Results; Conclusions (ssctr-evidence/PMC13670784.xml).
limitations: Small sample; men only; participants and trainers not blinded; retrospectively registered; eight weeks.
counterevidence: A lower set count costs some adaptation if it persists, so a reduction is acceptable only when it is short.

sources.title: The repeated bout effect of typical lower body strength training sessions on sub-maximal running performance and hormonal response
sources.authors: Doma K, Schumann M, Sinclair WH, Leicht AS, Deakin GB, Hakkinen K
sources.population_design_dose: 14 resistance-untrained men; two lower-body 6RM sessions one week apart; muscle damage markers and submaximal running at 24 and 48 h after each.
sources.findings: The second bout attenuated creatine kinase, soreness and the loss of jump height at 48 h; submaximal running was impaired for about 24 h after both bouts.
limitations: Abstract only; untrained men; 6RM sessions, far harder than 2 sets at RIR 3.
counterevidence: Running was impaired only up to about 24 h.

sources.title: The repeated bout effect of traditional resistance exercises on running performance across 3 bouts
sources.authors: Doma K, Schumann M, Leicht AS, Heilbronn BE, Damas F, Burt D
sources.population_design_dose: 12 resistance-untrained men; three lower-body 6RM sessions; damage markers and submaximal and maximal running at 24 and 48 h.
sources.findings: The first bout raised creatine kinase most; at least two bouts were needed before soreness, range of motion and submaximal running were protected; the authors advise avoiding submaximal running for at least 48 h after resistance training until the third bout.
limitations: Abstract only; untrained men; 6RM sessions.
counterevidence: Protection appeared after two bouts, so a single earlier block of training may already have conferred some.

sources.title: Comparison between high- and low-intensity eccentric cycling of equal mechanical work for muscle damage and the repeated bout effect
sources.authors: Mavropalias G, Koeda T, Barley OR, Poon WCK, Fisher AJ, Blazevich AJ, Nosaka K
sources.population_design_dose: 20 men; two eccentric cycling bouts 2 weeks apart: high-intensity twice (1 min x 5 at 20% of peak power, n = 11) or low-intensity first (4 min x 5 at 5% of peak power, matched mechanical work) then high-intensity (n = 9).
sources.findings: Both first bouts lowered knee-extensor torque and jump height similarly at 24 h, and both groups lost less function after the second bout. Soreness after the first bout was greater after high intensity (peak 4.2 vs 1.4), but after the second, high-intensity bout it was greater in the group whose first bout was low-intensity (3.6 vs 1.5).
limitations: Abstract only; eccentric cycling, not resistance training; allocation method not stated in the abstract; small groups; men only.
counterevidence: A low-intensity first bout protected function but gave less protection against soreness than a full first bout; soreness after the second bout (3.6) stayed below that after an unprotected high-intensity first bout (4.2).

sources.title: Knee position sense and knee flexor neuromuscular function are similarly altered after two submaximal eccentric bouts
sources.authors: Da Silva F, Monjo F, Gioda J, Blain GM, Piponnier E, Corcelle B, Colson SS
sources.population_design_dose: 16 participants; two submaximal unilateral knee-flexor eccentric bouts one week apart, each to a 20% loss of maximal isometric force.
sources.findings: No repeated-bout effect on neuromuscular function or position sense; soreness was present at 24 h.
limitations: Abstract only; fatigue-limited isolated eccentric bouts; outcomes are neuromuscular function and proprioception, not training adaptation; small sample.
counterevidence: A submaximal first bout need not protect at all on these outcomes.

claims.statement: Under reading A no exposure after a phase-reduced re-establishment exceeds the dose the approved rule already gives an exercise re-established with no recent bout at all (at most 2 sets at RIR >= 3, effort-guided under the earlier ceiling), and every later count is at most one set above the largest count executed since the re-establishment; the athlete has meanwhile had one more recent bout, whose protection persists for weeks (R6-S48) and is at least partial after a low-intensity bout (R6-S50, R6-S51). Reading A is therefore never less conservative than the approved first-bout rule.
claims.applicability: Recreational adults returning to an exercise after more than return.moderateMaxDays without it; low set counts at RIR >= 3.
limitations: Repeated-bout studies use eccentric or maximal protocols, mostly in young men; no study tests re-establishment schedules.
R6-S50 and R6-S51 are abstract-only and context only.
counterevidence: A reduced first bout protects less than a full one (R7A-S01) and a submaximal bout may not protect at all on some outcomes (R7A-S02); the dominance argument holds even with no protection.

claims.statement: A low-intensity first bout protected function but gave less protection against soreness than a full first bout; soreness after the second, larger bout stayed below that after an unprotected first bout (R7A-S01). Two submaximal eccentric bouts a week apart showed no repeated-bout effect on neuromuscular function and position sense (R7A-S02).
claims.applicability: Indirect: eccentric cycling and isolated eccentric bouts, not resistance training sets.
limitations: Abstract only; small samples; different modalities.
counterevidence: R6-S50 and R6-S51 found 30-66% protection after low-intensity eccentric bouts.

claims.statement: In resistance-untrained men two or more bouts were needed before submaximal running was protected (R6-S55), and running was impaired for about 24 h after each early bout (R6-S54); this applies to the early exposures under both readings and does not distinguish them.
claims.applicability: Hybrid athletes whose strength and running days are close.
limitations: Abstract only; 6RM bouts, heavier than an RIR >= 3 re-establishment.
counterevidence: Submaximal running physiology is little changed after a strength session (R6-S53, recorded in round 12).

claims.statement: Reading B would let a phase reduction meant for one week also lower the counts of the following unreduced weeks, a double reduction that neither the policy text nor strengthReturnSets states; the extra week at the reduced count has no evidence of benefit.
claims.applicability: Set-count trajectories after consolidation, specific, taper, race-window and post-event weeks.
limitations: Structural argument; R6-S52 shows single sets give smaller gains than three, not the cost of one extra week.
counterevidence: Conservatism alone could favour B; SSCTR-04 rules that conservative does not mean automatically reducing training.

claims.statement: No study tests how fast the number of sets should return after weeks without an exercise; the regain rule stays a conservative heuristic, not a physiological threshold.
claims.applicability: All re-establishments.
limitations: Negative searches in rounds 11 and 12.

R7A1-SSCTR-r2 rationale: R7A1-SSCTR-r2 delta check: carries with condition 9 met for the end of the return cap (D57). The second cycle changed what a whole week is in one case. QE-R7A-14 made the review read a time-fitted row by its count before the fit, as the projection did; that removes two readings of one week, but in the less conservative direction for the cap. My condition 5 already says a week raises the cap only when its executed sets equal the count before the phase reduction, and a fitted row executed fewer. On R7A-FREEZE-2 the cap now ends while the athlete has executed 2 sets, and when time allows the count returns 2 to 4 at once, which strength.setsAfterReestablishment ("never at once"), PLANNED-PROGRESSION condition 14 and ROTATION condition 10 ("never two at once") and my condition 6 exclude. After a performed re-establishment by effort (more than return.moderateMaxDays since the last executed exposure), the earlier count, block-boundary set included, comes back at most one set per executed week, never at once, whatever the state mode at the re-establishment (known load, pending establishment log, unlogged or re-established) (D53, resolved).

The regain base is the re-establishment count before its phase reduction: min(goal sets for the role, 2, the count the exercise would otherwise have that day). A re-establishment reduced by its phase is followed by that count itself, as a phase-reduced return step 2 is followed by the step-2 count (Q1, reading A).

The cap rises by one set only after a week whose last executed exposure of the exercise executed its whole count (executed sets equal to its count before the phase reduction, gate ADVANCE or EARNED, a logged set); a week whose executed row was below that count, by its phase or by an in-week fatigue reduction, never raises it. A phase week whose reduction did not bring the row below that count counts as a whole executed week.
Every later count stays at or below the cap, with phase reductions on top, and is never more than one set above the largest count executed since the re-establishment.
Load: a logged load at or after the re-establishment becomes the reference only by the existing adoption rules, never above the re-establishment ceiling (D44, D45).
To be declared in the next policy revision: setsAfterReestablishment states the base before the phase reduction and the whole-count rule, in the words of strengthReturnSets.

D56 (final formulation, R7A1-SSCTR-r1 S1): a time-budget fit is not a phase reduction, but a week executed its whole count only when the last executed exposure of the exercise that week, the one that gives the week’s counts (R19, INV-04), executed its count before the phase reduction after its time fit. Any other week neither raises nor ends the regain cap (after a re-establishment) or the return cap (at and after the end of the return steps); the return ceiling (lastExecutedSets) is the largest whole count executed after the fit (R20). Met at R7A1-FREEZE-A1 for the rise of both caps and for the regain cap; met at R7A1-FREEZE-A2 for the end of the return cap too (D57 closed). D57 (met at R7A1-FREEZE-A2 and at R7A2-FREEZE-1 and at R7A-FINAL-FREEZE and at R7A-BOUNDARY-FINAL-FREEZE and at STATE-EVIDENCE-FREEZE-1 and at HISTORICAL-PROJECTION-FREEZE-1): the return cap rises and ends only after a week whose last executed exposure did its whole count after its time fit, and ends only when it is at or above next week’s normal count with the block-boundary set that transition earns (phase reductions on top); the regain cap ends only at the largest count the exercise can have. No count after a re-establishment or a return exceeds the largest count executed since then by more than one set, for every exercise a cap or the return steps cover (B = 0 over the 864 and 360 timelines of my grids). The end test reads next week’s count as this week’s normal count plus the block set; another rise of the normal count at a transition (the NONE-class first-block clamp, a priorSets regain) was not reached with a cap in force (observation N4). Regression: the grid’s A, B and C at 0 and test "R7-A.1 D57" (both parts).

D59 (met at R7A2-FREEZE-1 and at R7A-FINAL-FREEZE and at R7A-BOUNDARY-FINAL-FREEZE and at STATE-EVIDENCE-FREEZE-1 and at HISTORICAL-PROJECTION-FREEZE-1, closed): a return starts from the state at the break (stateAtBreak, strengthAtBreak): every exercise executed before the break’s first day is in use with its last performed date and, outside a return step and a phase reduction, its last executed whole count after the time fit (target met) as the ceiling (the largest of the break week, R20); a moderate or long return enters it at strengthEntrySets with strengthEntryMinimumRir or more, step 2 follows, the block in progress earns no set and the count comes back at most one set per executed whole week up to the ceiling; the progression the pre-break exposures earned stays unapplied. Regression: ssctr-r7a1-recheck-firstweek.mjs with E, O and B at 0 for NONE and FAMILIAR and O at 0 for KNOWN, my restoration, cap and short grids, and test "R7-A.2 I4/I5/I8 (SSCTR D59)". R7ASE-SSCTR-r1: the state at the break also takes the load the athlete lifted on a known-load row as the exercise’s load (lighter, or heavier only under D44: at most one smallest increment above the row and the row’s target met), a fact and never a step; an effort-guided row adopts nothing; a projected dose lifted exactly is that load with its repetition target and no further step. This approval excludes a stored load tick that counts an exposure the projection assumed and the athlete did not execute (NF-R7ASE-3, R42).

R7A1-SSCTR-r1: R7A1-FREEZE-A1: adequate for the regain cap; the return-cap end is D57 (Earlier: Yes: the re-establishment envelope is adequate at this runtime for every state mode; the one-set-per-week regain holds and the event doses hold (record R7A-SSCTR-REESTABLISH-PHASE).)
The material fact is a performed re-establishment after more than return.moderateMaxDays without the exercise, with its executed count and logged set from the weekly review (completed-work ledger).
KEEP of the runtime is defensible; unknown is how much protection a reduced first bout leaves for this athlete.
Against reading B, reading A changes the count one week sooner after a phase-reduced re-establishment; neither changes the re-establishment dose itself.
The smallest sufficient rule is reading A with the whole-count condition; no runtime change.
Reading B adds a week at one set with no evidence of benefit and double-counts a one-week phase reduction; a fixed hold would ignore executed work.
It protects progression and the stated priority: the count returns at most one set per executed week and never above the approved first-bout dose.

Applicable evidence supports a gradual return after a gap and partial protection from a recent bout (R6-S48, R6-S50, R6-S51); counterevidence (R7A-S01, R7A-S02) does not defeat the dominance argument; no dose number is invented.
R7ASM-SSCTR-r1: material uncertainty remains in real use (synthetic probes only); Uncertain: individual protection after a 1-set bout; the regain schedule itself is a heuristic (RB-5).
No ASK, HOLD or clinical routing is needed for this nonclinical rule; clinical pauses route as before.

sources.title: Acute Neuromuscular, Physiological and Performance Responses After Strength Training in Runners: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
sources.authors: de Carvalho e Silva GI, Brandao LHA, dos Santos Silva D, de Jesus Alves MD, Aidar FJ, et al.
sources.population_design_dose: 19 studies (13 meta-analysed) of male runners; one strength session (traditional, explosive, plyometric or combined) before running tests, mostly 24-48 h later.
sources.findings: After a strength session peak torque fell and soreness, creatine kinase and perceived exertion rose; jump height, ventilation, oxygen uptake, lactate and heart rate were not different, and submaximal running was little affected; time to exhaustion fell in three of the four studies that measured it. The authors advise care to limit muscle damage before competition.
sources.locator: Abstract; Key Points; Results (time to exhaustion in four studies); Discussion; Practical Implications (ssctr-evidence/PMC9385928.xml).
limitations: Male participants only; small heterogeneous studies, several with damaging or 6RM protocols; no study of a taper or of a low-dose session.
counterevidence: Submaximal running physiology at 24 h was largely unchanged after strength sessions, even after damaging protocols.

sources.title: Effects of tapering on performance in endurance athletes: A systematic review and meta-analysis
sources.authors: Wang Z, Wang YT, Gao W, Zhong Y
sources.population_design_dose: 14 studies in well-trained endurance athletes (VO2max >55 ml/kg/min).
sources.findings: Taper improved time-trial (SMD -0.45) and time-to-exhaustion performance; volume reductions of 41-60% with maintained intensity and frequency, durations <=7, 8-14 or 15-21 days and progressive or step tapers were effective.
limitations: Trained, not recreational, athletes; few studies per subgroup.
counterevidence: No change in VO2max or economy; benefits depend on prior overload.

sources.title: The Duration of the Repeated-Bout Effect After Eccentric Exercise
sources.authors: Theodorou AA, Margaritelis NV, Karyofyllidou AV, Christodoulou F, Jamurtas AZ, et al.
sources.population_design_dose: 48 young recreationally active men; two identical bouts of maximal eccentric knee-extensor exercise (5 x 15 repetitions); after the first bout participants were randomly allocated to repeat it after 3, 6, 9 or 12 weeks (12 completers per group).
sources.findings: The repeated-bout effect (smaller losses of torque and range of motion, less soreness and muscle damage) was evident at 3 and 6 weeks for most outcomes, remained detectable at 9 weeks for selected markers, and was no longer meaningfully present at 12 weeks.
sources.locator: Abstract; Methods 2.2 (random allocation to the interval groups); Results (Table 2, model-estimated contrasts by interval); Discussion (earlier downhill-running and elbow-flexor studies); Limitations (ssctr-evidence/PMC13674372.xml).
limitations: Maximal unaccustomed eccentric knee-extensor work in young men; resistance training at 2-3 reps in reserve damages muscle far less; markers assessed on days 2 and 4 only; activity between bouts not monitored.
counterevidence: Earlier studies cited in the discussion found protection that faded by 9 weeks after downhill running and persisted partly to 10 weeks for the elbow flexors.

sources.title: Comparative effects of single vs. multiple-set resistance training on neuromuscular performance and muscle morphology in sedentary men
sources.authors: Coskun IA, Kafkas ME
sources.population_design_dose: 34 sedentary young men randomized (computer-generated sequence, sealed opaque envelopes) to single-set, three-set or control; 8 weeks, twice weekly, seven exercises of up to 10 repetitions.
sources.findings: Both single-set and three-set training improved strength, power and muscle size over 8 weeks; three sets gave larger gains (squat 1-RM +14.8% and leg cross-sectional area +11.3%, against about 6-8% with one set), a volume dose-response from the first weeks.
sources.locator: Abstract; Methods (randomization, concealed allocation, training programme); Results; Conclusions (ssctr-evidence/PMC13670784.xml).
limitations: Small sample; men only; participants and trainers not blinded; retrospectively registered; eight weeks.
counterevidence: A lower set count costs some adaptation if it persists, so a reduction is acceptable only when it is short.

sources.title: Effects of Short-Term Concurrent Training Cessation on the Energy Cost of Running and Neuromuscular Performances in Middle-Distance Runners
sources.authors: Berryman N, Mujika I, Bosquet L
sources.population_design_dose: 8 middle-distance runners; 8 weeks of plyometric or dynamic weight training added to running, then 4 weeks of running only; no control group.
sources.findings: The improved energy cost of running was kept after 4 weeks without strength training, and the 3000 m time trial improved further (-4.4% from baseline); the authors suggest that stopping explosive strength training could serve as a taper strategy.
sources.locator: Abstract; Discussion (limitations: small sample, no control intervention); Conclusions (ssctr-evidence/PMC7821917.xml).
limitations: Brief report; 8 runners; no control group; explosive strength only.
counterevidence: Strength kept at a low dose through the taper is not tested against stopping it.

Directed PubMed search for evidence that a reduced first bout does not protect (two abstracts read, both recorded as counterevidence); round-1 to round-12 sources and searches reused as recorded there. Search snippets were discovery only; findings are taken from full text or, where labelled, abstracts. R7A2-SSCTR-r1: Two directed PubMed searches (minimal effective strength dose; training cessation), counterevidence sought in the same queries (R7A2-S01: a single set is "suboptimal"; R6-S52 full text: a lower set count costs adaptation if it persists). R7AF-SSCTR-r1 (regression only): access and currency confirmed by two PubMed searches limited to 2025-2026 syntheses; titles listed, none read, none relied on. Counterevidence to the delta was sought by probing the frozen runtime against R7A2-FREEZE-1 on every changed path (ssctr-r7af-probe.mjs, ssctr-r7af-sameday.mjs). R7AB-SSCTR-r1 (regression only): access and currency confirmed by the same two PubMed searches (no new hit). Counterevidence to the delta was sought by probing the frozen runtime against the byte-exact R7A-FINAL-FREEZE copy on every changed path, with controls and an isolation case (ssctr-r7ab-probe.mjs). Counterevidence to the delta was sought by probing the frozen runtime against the byte-exact R7A-BOUNDARY-FINAL-FREEZE copy on every changed path, each unreviewed cell against its reviewed control (ssctr-r7ase-probe.mjs, ssctr-r7ase-systemic-probe.mjs, ssctr-r7ase-tick-probe.mjs, my b-probe), and by my own regression comparison with the return entry not ignored (ssctr-r7ase-regression-probe.mjs, ssctr-r7ase-holdout-detail.mjs).

claims.statement: A strength session lowers peak torque and raises soreness, creatine kinase and perceived exertion in runners for 24-48 h (R6-S53), and tapers that cut volume while keeping intensity improve endurance performance (R6-S14); a re-establishment near an event therefore takes the reduced event dose like any other row, and a first bout after more than four weeks, whose repeated-bout protection has partly faded (R6-S48), never gets more.
claims.applicability: Taper, race-window and post-event strength sessions of recreational hybrid runners.
limitations: Trained endurance athletes in R6-S14; male runners in R6-S53; no taper study of strength re-establishment.
counterevidence: Submaximal running physiology was little changed after a strength session (R6-S53).

claims.statement: Single-set training still improved strength, power and muscle size, with smaller gains than three sets (R6-S52); a 1-set re-establishment in a consolidation or specific week, or for an exercise whose own count is 1, is a lower but real stimulus inside a planned step-back, so taking the phase dose costs at most a small, temporary stimulus.
claims.applicability: Re-establishment rows outside event phases (Q2).
limitations: Sedentary young men over 8 weeks; chronic adaptation, not a single week.
counterevidence: Three sets gave larger gains (R6-S52).

claims.statement: Stopping strength training for the final weeks did not hurt running economy or a 3000 m time in a small uncontrolled study (R6-S56).
claims.applicability: Event phases.
limitations: 8 runners, no control group; not eligible as prescriptive support.
counterevidence: None located.

claims.statement: No study tests a strength re-establishment or any strength dose inside a running taper.
claims.applicability: Taper and race-window re-establishments.
limitations: Round-12 negative search, reused.
counterevidence: None located.

records.applicability: Runtime composition rule inside the approved EVENT-TRANSITION and LOAD-ESTABLISHMENT envelopes, offline synthetic Node24 reference; no real-athlete effect.

decision.rationale: R7ASM-SSCTR-r1 delta check: carries: the round-12 phase and re-establishment sections are equal; D52 is now measured from executed dates (round-12 AF: 8 planned-date audit violations on the predecessor, 0 here; a 49-day gap re-establishes by effort under the last executed 82.5 kg where the predecessor prescribed a never-lifted 87.5 kg); bodyweight rows after a long gap take the executed repetitions (Z_D52, Y2_D51). R7ASE-SSCTR-r1 delta check: carries unchanged: the re-establishment phase readings are untouched. R7AB-SSCTR-r1 delta check: carries unchanged: the re-establishment phase readings are untouched; the one changed section is the start state of a never-logged return (S-C). R7AF-SSCTR-r1 delta check: carries unchanged. R7A2-SSCTR-r1 rationale: R7A2-SSCTR-r1 delta check: carries unchanged. R7A1-SSCTR-r2 rationale: R7A1-SSCTR-r2 delta check: carries unchanged. R7A1-SSCTR-r1 rationale: R7A1-SSCTR-r1 delta check: carries unchanged; the phase reading of the re-establishment row and the event bounds are unchanged, and the S9 rule re-plans remaining days under their new day phase. Earlier rationale (R7A-SSCTR-r2): D54 and the Q2 ruling carry unchanged: the second cycle did not change the single phase composition point, and my phase grid, the instrument’s AK section and the S4 event cases give the R7A-FREEZE-1 results or better. Re-bound to R7A-FREEZE-2 with the same conditions.
preserve: Effort-guided load under the earlier ceiling at a re-establishment
The event doses of operational.event and the consolidation reduction
decision.mec_change_level: No runtime or policy change; the single phase composition point as frozen.
decision.trade_off: A smaller re-establishment stimulus in reduced weeks, against a first bout after a gap at the full re-establishment dose in the window the reduced dose exists for.
must_not: Present any value as validated physiology, an injury-prevention threshold, a readiness score or a guarantee.
Substitute a training dose for clinical assessment.
Treat missing data as adverse or as tolerance.
Change official plan state or completed history.
conditions: Scope: offline synthetic Node24 reference only, for the adult (18+) recreational nonclinical V1 population stated in PROGRAM_POLICY_R6.population. Missing current eligibility is ASK; pain, injury, illness, functional limitation or a clinical interruption reason is CLINICAL_HUMAN_REQUIRED with no substitute dose.

Any change to a bound file needs a new freeze revision and a narrow runtime delta check; any policy byte change needs a delta binding review.

Every strength row, the re-establishment row included, takes its day phase once: sets = min(row cap, phase dose of the count the exercise would otherwise have that day), reps in reserve >= max(row floor, phase minimum); the day phase follows days to the race (proximitySemantics).

Race window and post-event: main lifts only, at most raceWeekStrengthSets / postEventStrengthSets set(s) at RIR >= raceWeekStrengthMinimumRir; one race-window session at most, on the strength day furthest from the race and none in the last raceWeekStrengthMinDaysBeforeRace days. Taper and specific rows keep RIR >= 3 (D54, resolved).

A re-establishment row is never above min(goal sets for its role, 2) and never above the phase dose of the exercise's own count that day; it may be below min(goal sets, 2) when that phase dose or the exercise's own count is lower (consolidation, specific, a known dose of 1 set) (Q2).
At a re-establishment the load stays effort-guided under the earlier ceiling; no load increase, new exercise or rotation in taper or race week.
The final validation rejects any strength row above its day phase dose or below the phase minimum reps in reserve, whatever branch built it.

D59 (met at R7A2-FREEZE-1 and at R7A-FINAL-FREEZE and at R7A-BOUNDARY-FINAL-FREEZE and at STATE-EVIDENCE-FREEZE-1 and at HISTORICAL-PROJECTION-FREEZE-1, closed): a return starts from the state at the break (stateAtBreak, strengthAtBreak): every exercise executed before the break’s first day is in use with its last performed date and, outside a return step and a phase reduction, its last executed whole count after the time fit (target met) as the ceiling (the largest of the break week, R20); a moderate or long return enters it at strengthEntrySets with strengthEntryMinimumRir or more, step 2 follows, the block in progress earns no set and the count comes back at most one set per executed whole week up to the ceiling; the progression the pre-break exposures earned stays unapplied. Regression: ssctr-r7a1-recheck-firstweek.mjs with E, O and B at 0 for NONE and FAMILIAR and O at 0 for KNOWN, my restoration, cap and short grids, and test "R7-A.2 I4/I5/I8 (SSCTR D59)". R7ASE-SSCTR-r1: the state at the break also takes the load the athlete lifted on a known-load row as the exercise’s load (lighter, or heavier only under D44: at most one smallest increment above the row and the row’s target met), a fact and never a step; an effort-guided row adopts nothing; a projected dose lifted exactly is that load with its repetition target and no further step. This approval excludes a stored load tick that counts an exposure the projection assumed and the athlete did not execute (NF-R7ASE-3, R42).

The start state of a return is the state at its interruption under R7A2-SSCTR-INTERRUPTION-STATE (revision R7ASM-SSCTR-r1), INTERRUPTION_EPISODE_CONTRACT R7AF-INTERRUPTION-1, WEEK_START_AUTHORITY_CONTRACT R7AB-WEEKSTART-1 (its record, temporal-contradiction rule and boundaries B1-B7, B9-B11) and STATE_MODEL_CONTRACT R7ASM-STATE-MODEL-1 (which replaces STATE_EVIDENCE_CONTRACT R7ASE-STATE-EVIDENCE-1): a correction names its interruption (episodeId) or repeats its days and starts from what the athlete had executed at its own start; a break after a re-entry or after training is new and starts from that re-entry plus the facts executed since; the state at the interruption is read value by value (one value per strength exercise, one for the run): a stored value counts only when its start holds that value as evidence decided before the cut (the intake, a return’s entry, the weekly review’s rule on that value’s historical value, or a projection whose own base value was historical and that the week before executed per sport exactly as assumed, loads included); a value a review carried from a projection is rebuilt by the review’s rule on its historical value; otherwise the value moves back to its last such start and the sessions executed after it are facts only (a known load lifted is the load under D44; a projected dose lifted is that load with its repetition target, never a load tick only the projection counted); weeks never reported are not history; a named correction that contradicts its own executed re-entry is asked; anything else is asked; each short break owns its easy slot.

Weekly-review contract: these bindings hold when every elapsed week receives a gating weekly review, in order and after its last session, with unreported sessions reviewed as missed. A week that receives no gating review keeps the projection's assumption that it was executed and logged (establishment, progression, block credit, achieved peaks and the strength resume clock); that path is outside this approval and must be closed before any use beyond the offline reference (R18).

confidence.rationale: R7ASM-SSCTR-r1: the grids and probes this record rests on were re-run on both runtimes. Behaviour verified on both runtimes over a wider grid than round 12, with twins and an independent reduction formula; the dose rationale rests on indirect acute and taper evidence.

limitations: Synthetic timelines only.
No direct study of strength re-establishment near an event.
R7ASM-SSCTR-r1: synthetic offline probes only; the findings are demonstrated on my own scenarios and on the corpus, not on real athletes.

answers.answer: At HISTORICAL-PROJECTION-FREEZE-1: adequate for this record's scope (its grids and probes hold, see the rationale); the freeze as a whole is NOT_READY on F1, F2 and F3. At STATE-EVIDENCE-FREEZE-1: adequate; the value-scoped history leaves the planner, the return recipe, ceilings, restoration and short return unchanged (byte-identical grids; R5, profiles and simulations identical) and only changes which executed state a return starts from. At R7A-BOUNDARY-FINAL-FREEZE: adequate; the week-start authority change leaves the return recipe, ceilings, restoration and short return unchanged (byte-identical grids) and only moves a return's start back to an executed state. At R7A-FINAL-FREEZE: adequate; the identity and state change leaves the return recipe, ceilings, restoration and short return unchanged (byte-identical grids). R7A2-SSCTR-r1: At R7A2-FREEZE-1: adequate; the start state of a return is the state at the break (D59 closed). R7A1-SSCTR-r2: At R7A1-FREEZE-A2: adequate; the start state of a return is outside this record (D59). R7A1-SSCTR-r1: R7A1-FREEZE-A1: unchanged (Earlier: Yes: with the event doses applied to the re-establishment row the event envelope is adequate at this runtime.)
The material facts are the session date relative to the race (day phase) and the exercise's own count that day.
KEEP of the runtime is defensible; unknown is the individual response to a first bout after a gap near a race.
The comparator is the round-12 runtime (2 sets at RIR 3 in race week, post-event and taper); the reduced dose is necessary to meet principle 8 and operational.event.
The smallest sufficient change is the one composition point already implemented; no new rule.
Leaving the row unreduced contradicts the declared event doses; skipping the exercise would lose the movement for the event block with no evidence that a light set harms.
It protects the event priority and keeps strength at a reduced maintenance dose.

sources.title: The Duration of the Repeated-Bout Effect After Eccentric Exercise
sources.authors: Theodorou AA, Margaritelis NV, Karyofyllidou AV, Christodoulou F, Jamurtas AZ, et al.
sources.population_design_dose: 48 young recreationally active men; two identical bouts of maximal eccentric knee-extensor exercise (5 x 15 repetitions); after the first bout participants were randomly allocated to repeat it after 3, 6, 9 or 12 weeks (12 completers per group).
sources.findings: The repeated-bout effect (smaller losses of torque and range of motion, less soreness and muscle damage) was evident at 3 and 6 weeks for most outcomes, remained detectable at 9 weeks for selected markers, and was no longer meaningfully present at 12 weeks.
sources.locator: Abstract; Methods 2.2 (random allocation to the interval groups); Results (Table 2, model-estimated contrasts by interval); Discussion (earlier downhill-running and elbow-flexor studies); Limitations (ssctr-evidence/PMC13674372.xml).
limitations: Maximal unaccustomed eccentric knee-extensor work in young men; resistance training at 2-3 reps in reserve damages muscle far less; markers assessed on days 2 and 4 only; activity between bouts not monitored.
counterevidence: Earlier studies cited in the discussion found protection that faded by 9 weeks after downhill running and persisted partly to 10 weeks for the elbow flexors.

claims.statement: An exposure executed at the known dose within return.moderateMaxDays of the previous one keeps the athlete exposed: the repeated-bout protection of a bout persists for weeks (R6-S48), so a later row of that week dated beyond the window does not turn the week into a first bout after a gap; the known state and count stand.
claims.applicability: Exercises prescribed more than once a week.
limitations: Eccentric protocol in young men; the 28-day window is a declared operational value, not a threshold.
counterevidence: Protection fades over weeks and differs by outcome (R6-S48).

claims.statement: Reading the return ceiling from the largest whole count executed in the week (R20) never exceeds a count actually executed and removes the one-set-low ceiling of a week whose known row was executed before a lower re-establishment row; reading the cap rise from the same whole set keeps every later count at most one set above a count executed.
claims.applicability: Split weeks in every phase.
limitations: Structural reasoning on the declared rule.
counterevidence: Reading only the last executed row errs one set low (R7A-SSCTR-r1, R20); reading a fitted row by its count before the fit errs high (D56).

records.applicability: Runtime state-transition rule inside the approved LOAD-ESTABLISHMENT and ROTATION envelopes, offline synthetic Node24 reference; no real-athlete effect.

decision.rationale: R7ASM-SSCTR-r1 delta check: carries: the week's counts still come from what it executed (grids and probes). R7ASE-SSCTR-r1 delta check: carries: the week’s counts still come from what it executed. R7AB-SSCTR-r1 delta check: carries: the week’s counts still come from what it executed. R7AF-SSCTR-r1 delta check: carries; R20 unchanged. R7A2-SSCTR-r1 rationale: R7A2-SSCTR-r1 delta check: carries; R20 now also defines the ceiling read from the break week. R7A1-SSCTR-r2 rationale: R7A1-SSCTR-r2 delta check: carries unchanged. R7A1-SSCTR-r1 rationale: R7A1-SSCTR-r1 delta check: carries with condition 4 amended to the final D56 formulation ("the last executed exposure"), now met. Earlier rationale (R7A-SSCTR-r2): R19 and the first-executed-exposure rule carry unchanged. My R20 is adopted: the return ceiling is the largest whole count executed in the week, after the time fit, which removes the one-set-low ceiling of the both-executed case without exceeding any count executed. Condition 4 is amended to that reading, and the cap rise is aligned with it: a week moves the regain or return cap only when one of its executed exposures executed its whole count after the fit (D56, open at R7A-FREEZE-2).
preserve: Each session judged on its own date; no unexecuted exposure counts (LE-15)
modify: Condition 4 amended: the return ceiling and the cap rise read the week’s whole executed counts after the time fit (R20 adopted; D56 required).
decision.mec_change_level: No policy change; R20 as frozen; D56 required for the cap rise.
decision.trade_off: A known count kept after a demonstrated exposure, against a possible one-set-low return ceiling when both rows are executed.

A week re-established an exercise only when its first executed exposure that week was a re-establishment row; a known-dose exposure executed first keeps the state known at its count, with no conversion and no regain cap, whatever later rows of that week prescribe (R19, resolved).

The week’s counts come from what it executed: the return ceiling is the largest whole count executed that week outside a phase reduction, each exposure counted after its time fit (R20, met); the regain and return caps rise only after a week whose last executed exposure, the one that gives the week’s counts (condition 3, R19), executed its whole count after its time fit (D56 final formulation, R7A1-SSCTR-r1 S1, met at R7A1-FREEZE-A1 and at R7A1-FREEZE-A2 and at R7A2-FREEZE-1 and at R7A-FINAL-FREEZE and at R7A-BOUNDARY-FINAL-FREEZE and at STATE-EVIDENCE-FREEZE-1 and at HISTORICAL-PROJECTION-FREEZE-1); a prescribed but unexecuted row never decides.
A logged load is judged against the exposure it was logged in, under the earlier ceiling when that exposure was a re-establishment (D44, D45).

D59 (met at R7A2-FREEZE-1 and at R7A-FINAL-FREEZE and at R7A-BOUNDARY-FINAL-FREEZE and at STATE-EVIDENCE-FREEZE-1 and at HISTORICAL-PROJECTION-FREEZE-1, closed): a return starts from the state at the break (stateAtBreak, strengthAtBreak): every exercise executed before the break’s first day is in use with its last performed date and, outside a return step and a phase reduction, its last executed whole count after the time fit (target met) as the ceiling (the largest of the break week, R20); a moderate or long return enters it at strengthEntrySets with strengthEntryMinimumRir or more, step 2 follows, the block in progress earns no set and the count comes back at most one set per executed whole week up to the ceiling; the progression the pre-break exposures earned stays unapplied. This approval excludes a stored load tick that counts an exposure the projection assumed and the athlete did not execute (NF-R7ASE-3, R42).

The start state of a return is the state at its interruption under R7A2-SSCTR-INTERRUPTION-STATE (revision R7ASM-SSCTR-r1), INTERRUPTION_EPISODE_CONTRACT R7AF-INTERRUPTION-1, WEEK_START_AUTHORITY_CONTRACT R7AB-WEEKSTART-1 (its record, temporal-contradiction rule and boundaries B1-B7, B9-B11) and STATE_MODEL_CONTRACT R7ASM-STATE-MODEL-1 (which replaces STATE_EVIDENCE_CONTRACT R7ASE-STATE-EVIDENCE-1): a correction names its interruption (episodeId) or repeats its days and starts from what the athlete had executed at its own start; a break after a re-entry or after training is new and starts from that re-entry plus the facts executed since; the state at the interruption is read value by value (one value per strength exercise, one for the run): a stored value counts only when its start holds that value as evidence decided before the cut (the intake, a return’s entry, the weekly review’s rule on that value’s historical value, or a projection whose own base value was historical and that the week before executed per sport exactly as assumed, loads included); a value a review carried from a projection is rebuilt by the review’s rule on its historical value; otherwise the value moves back to its last such start and the sessions executed after it are facts only (a known load lifted is the load under D44; a projected dose lifted is that load with its repetition target, never a load tick only the projection counted); weeks never reported are not history; a named correction that contradicts its own executed re-entry is asked; anything else is asked; each short break owns its easy slot.

Weekly-review contract: these bindings hold when every elapsed week receives a gating weekly review, in order and after its last session, with unreported sessions reviewed as missed. A week that receives no gating review keeps the projection's assumption that it was executed and logged (establishment, progression, block credit, achieved peaks and the strength resume clock); that path is outside this approval and must be closed before any use beyond the offline reference (R18).

KEEP of the known state is defensible; unknown is whether the later effort-guided row was needed at all.
Against the round-12 runtime, which converted the state on the last prescribed row, no change is necessary after a demonstrated known exposure.
The smallest sufficient rule is the executed-exposure reading already implemented.
A conversion or cap after a demonstrated known exposure would cut the count with no gap to justify it.
It protects progression without skipping the regain when the re-establishment is the exposure actually performed.
Repeated-bout evidence supports treating a recent executed exposure as protective; no number is invented.

sources.title: American College of Sports Medicine Position Stand. Resistance Training Prescription for Muscle Function, Hypertrophy, and Physical Performance in Healthy Adults: An Overview of Reviews
sources.authors: Currier BS, D'Souza AC, Singh MAF, Lowisz CV, Rawson ES, Schoenfeld BJ, Smith-Ryan AE, et al.
sources.population_design_dose: Overview of 137 systematic reviews of randomized trials in healthy adults (>=18 y), resistance training >=6 wk; most evidence from novice trainees.
sources.findings: Resistance training improves strength and hypertrophy versus control; strength enhanced by heavier loads, 2-3 sets, >=2 sessions/wk and exercise at session start; hypertrophy by >=10 sets/muscle/wk; training to failure and periodization not consistently influential; perceived-exertion scales can raise absolute load with strength gains; individualization encouraged for adherence.
sources.locator: Abstract; Results (strength, hypertrophy); Discussion subsections Progressive overload, Specificity/Individualization, Variation.
limitations: Overview of reviews dominated by novice trainees; not concurrent-training or runner specific.
No per-session increment, establishment or return procedure is specified.
counterevidence: States progression is not always necessary for benefit, so planned progression is a choice, not a requirement.

sources.title: Monitoring the athlete training response: subjective self-reported measures trump commonly used objective measures: a systematic review
sources.authors: Saw AE, Main LC, Gastin PB
sources.population_design_dose: 56 studies reporting concurrent subjective and objective athlete well-being measures.
sources.findings: Subjective measures reflected acute and chronic training load with better sensitivity and consistency than objective measures.
limitations: Athletes; measure heterogeneity.
counterevidence: Subjective and objective measures often did not correlate.

sources.title: Acute Neuromuscular, Physiological and Performance Responses After Strength Training in Runners: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
sources.authors: de Carvalho e Silva GI, Brandao LHA, dos Santos Silva D, de Jesus Alves MD, Aidar FJ, et al.
sources.population_design_dose: 19 studies (13 meta-analysed) of male runners; one strength session (traditional, explosive, plyometric or combined) before running tests, mostly 24-48 h later.
sources.findings: After a strength session peak torque fell and soreness, creatine kinase and perceived exertion rose; jump height, ventilation, oxygen uptake, lactate and heart rate were not different, and submaximal running was little affected; time to exhaustion fell in three of the four studies that measured it. The authors advise care to limit muscle damage before competition.
sources.locator: Abstract; Key Points; Results (time to exhaustion in four studies); Discussion; Practical Implications (ssctr-evidence/PMC9385928.xml).
limitations: Male participants only; small heterogeneous studies, several with damaging or 6RM protocols; no study of a taper or of a low-dose session.
counterevidence: Submaximal running physiology at 24 h was largely unchanged after strength sessions, even after damaging protocols.

sources.title: Gaining more from doing less? The effects of a one-week deload period during supervised resistance training on muscular adaptations
sources.authors: Coleman M, Burke R, Augustin F, Pinero A, Maldonado J, Fisher JP, Israetel M, et al.
sources.population_design_dose: 39 resistance-trained young men and women; 9-week high-volume program; one group abstained from training for 1 week at the midpoint and then resumed the same program, the other trained continuously.
sources.findings: No appreciable between-group differences in lower-body muscle size, local endurance or power; the continuous group improved isometric and dynamic lower-body strength more than the deload group.
sources.locator: Abstract; Methods (group allocation, deload at the midpoint); Results; Limitations (ssctr-evidence/PMC10809978.xml).
limitations: The deload was complete cessation, not a set reduction; resistance-trained young adults; upper-body training unsupervised.
counterevidence: Strength gains were smaller after one week without training, so breaks are not neutral for strength.

sources.title: Effects of tapering on performance in endurance athletes: A systematic review and meta-analysis
sources.authors: Wang Z, Wang YT, Gao W, Zhong Y
sources.population_design_dose: 14 studies in well-trained endurance athletes (VO2max >55 ml/kg/min).
sources.findings: Taper improved time-trial (SMD -0.45) and time-to-exhaustion performance; volume reductions of 41-60% with maintained intensity and frequency, durations <=7, 8-14 or 15-21 days and progressive or step tapers were effective.
limitations: Trained, not recreational, athletes; few studies per subgroup.
counterevidence: No change in VO2max or economy; benefits depend on prior overload.

sources.title: The Duration of the Repeated-Bout Effect After Eccentric Exercise
sources.authors: Theodorou AA, Margaritelis NV, Karyofyllidou AV, Christodoulou F, Jamurtas AZ, et al.
sources.population_design_dose: 48 young recreationally active men; two identical bouts of maximal eccentric knee-extensor exercise (5 x 15 repetitions); after the first bout participants were randomly allocated to repeat it after 3, 6, 9 or 12 weeks (12 completers per group).
sources.findings: The repeated-bout effect (smaller losses of torque and range of motion, less soreness and muscle damage) was evident at 3 and 6 weeks for most outcomes, remained detectable at 9 weeks for selected markers, and was no longer meaningfully present at 12 weeks.
sources.locator: Abstract; Methods 2.2 (random allocation to the interval groups); Results (Table 2, model-estimated contrasts by interval); Discussion (earlier downhill-running and elbow-flexor studies); Limitations (ssctr-evidence/PMC13674372.xml).
limitations: Maximal unaccustomed eccentric knee-extensor work in young men; resistance training at 2-3 reps in reserve damages muscle far less; markers assessed on days 2 and 4 only; activity between bouts not monitored.
counterevidence: Earlier studies cited in the discussion found protection that faded by 9 weeks after downhill running and persisted partly to 10 weeks for the elbow flexors.

sources.title: The repeated bout effect of typical lower body strength training sessions on sub-maximal running performance and hormonal response
sources.authors: Doma K, Schumann M, Sinclair WH, Leicht AS, Deakin GB, Hakkinen K
sources.population_design_dose: 14 resistance-untrained men; two lower-body 6RM sessions one week apart; muscle damage markers and submaximal running at 24 and 48 h after each.
sources.findings: The second bout attenuated creatine kinase, soreness and the loss of jump height at 48 h; submaximal running was impaired for about 24 h after both bouts.
limitations: Abstract only; untrained men; 6RM sessions, far harder than 2 sets at RIR 3.
counterevidence: Running was impaired only up to about 24 h.

sources.title: The repeated bout effect of traditional resistance exercises on running performance across 3 bouts
sources.authors: Doma K, Schumann M, Leicht AS, Heilbronn BE, Damas F, Burt D
sources.population_design_dose: 12 resistance-untrained men; three lower-body 6RM sessions; damage markers and submaximal and maximal running at 24 and 48 h.
sources.findings: The first bout raised creatine kinase most; at least two bouts were needed before soreness, range of motion and submaximal running were protected; the authors advise avoiding submaximal running for at least 48 h after resistance training until the third bout.
limitations: Abstract only; untrained men; 6RM sessions.
counterevidence: Protection appeared after two bouts, so a single earlier block of training may already have conferred some.

sources.title: Comparison between high- and low-intensity eccentric cycling of equal mechanical work for muscle damage and the repeated bout effect
sources.authors: Mavropalias G, Koeda T, Barley OR, Poon WCK, Fisher AJ, Blazevich AJ, Nosaka K
sources.population_design_dose: 20 men; two eccentric cycling bouts 2 weeks apart: high-intensity twice (1 min x 5 at 20% of peak power, n = 11) or low-intensity first (4 min x 5 at 5% of peak power, matched mechanical work) then high-intensity (n = 9).
sources.findings: Both first bouts lowered knee-extensor torque and jump height similarly at 24 h, and both groups lost less function after the second bout. Soreness after the first bout was greater after high intensity (peak 4.2 vs 1.4), but after the second, high-intensity bout it was greater in the group whose first bout was low-intensity (3.6 vs 1.5).
limitations: Abstract only; eccentric cycling, not resistance training; allocation method not stated in the abstract; small groups; men only.
counterevidence: A low-intensity first bout protected function but gave less protection against soreness than a full first bout; soreness after the second bout (3.6) stayed below that after an unprotected high-intensity first bout (4.2).
